questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Where do approximately 70% of brain tumors occur in adults?
options: Supratentorially (within the cerebral hemispheres or coverings)
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of brain tumors in adults occur supratentorially (within the cerebral hemispheres or their coverings). This includes gliomas, meningiomas, and metastatic tumors. Infratentorial (posterior fossa) tumors (B) are more common in children. The answer is A. The supratentorial location in adults reflects the higher incidence of gliomas and metastatic disease in the cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: Adult brain tumors are predominantly supratentorial (70%) - cerebral hemispheres are the most common location.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Where are pilocytic astrocytomas most commonly located?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas are most commonly located in the CEREBELLUM (posterior fossa). They also occur in optic pathways, brainstem, and spinal cord. The cerebellar location is classic, especially in children. The answer is B. This is the most common pediatric brain tumor and has excellent prognosis when completely resected.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma occurs most commonly in the cerebellum in children - excellent prognosis with resection.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Where is the supplementary motor area located?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located in the medial surface of frontal lobe, anterior to the primary motor cortex (area 4), in Brodmann area 6.
questions.keyConcept: SMA is medial frontal cortex involved in motor planning, located anterior to primary motor cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The representational hemisphere is described by which one of the following?
options: It always lies in left hemisphere
It is responsible for visuospatial relations
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere, usually right, is responsible for visuospatial relationships and perceiving the spatial positions of objects in the environment.
questions.keyConcept: Representational hemisphere: visuospatial relations (usually right).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The motor area 4 is:
options: Located in the post central gyrus in the frontal lobe.
Main site of origin of extrapyranidal tract.
The main cortical area responsible for control of fine discrete movements
questions.explanation: Motor area 4 is the main cortical area responsible for control of fine discrete movements. Option D is correct. Primary motor cortex (area 4) in the precentral gyrus is the main origin of corticospinal tract. Option A is wrong (area 4 is precentral, not postcentral). Option B is wrong (area 4 facilitates tone, not inhibits). Option C is wrong (pyramidal tract originates from area 4).
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4) in the precentral gyrus is the key area for fine, discrete voluntary movements.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
options: receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck
extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the CERVICAL spinal cord, not the whole length. It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination. It does not extend into the lumbosacral cord.
questions.keyConcept: MLF: brainstem to cervical cord; connects vestibular nuclei to control head/neck movements.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Choose the CORRECT statement:
options: In spinal cord, white matter is H-shaped.
In brain stem, white matter surrounds grey matter.
Cerebral hemispheres contain deep nuclei formed of grey matter.
In cerebellum, white matter forms the outer cortex.
In spinal cord, grey matter surrounds white matter.
questions.explanation: The cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei such as the basal ganglia and thalamus. In the spinal cord, grey matter is central and H-shaped. The brainstem has grey matter surrounded by white matter, and the cerebellar cortex is grey matter externally.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei; spinal cord grey matter is central, white matter peripheral

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the most common location for Ependymomas in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, ependymomas are most commonly located in the SPINAL CORD (particularly thoracolumbar). In children, they occur more often in the posterior fossa (fourth ventricle). The answer is A. Spinal ependymomas often present with pain and gradual neurological deficit. Complete surgical resection is often curative.
questions.keyConcept: Adult ependymomas occur most often in the spinal cord; pediatric ependymomas occur in the fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which part of the spinal cord is responsible for transmitting motor signals to the muscles that control fine movements of the fingers and hands?
questions.explanation: Fine movements of the fingers and hands are controlled by the C8-T1 spinal cord segments, which give rise to the ulnar and median nerves. The cervical region of the spinal cord (C5-T1) is enlarged at the cervicothoracic junction (intumescence) specifically to accommodate the large number of motor neurons for the upper limbs. The lumbar region controls the lower limbs.
questions.keyConcept: Finger/hand fine movements = CERVICAL spinal cord region (especially C8-T1); cervical enlargement supplies upper limb nerves.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Infection spreads from suppurative lung diseases to the brain via:
questions.explanation: Infection spreads from suppurative lung diseases (lung abscess, bronchiectasis) to the brain via vertebral veins (Batson's venous plexus), which connects the pelvic veins to the intracranial venous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Lung infection spreads to brain via vertebral veins (Batson's plexus)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nerve that carries the sensation for the lower eyelid is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the upper eyelid and forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from the lower eyelid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of sensation from lower eye lid indicates injury of:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits through the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. Loss of sensation indicates injury to this nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid skin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The 2 frontal bellies:
options: Form the only muscle of face.
Are attached to superior temporal line.
questions.explanation: The two frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle originate from the skin of the eyebrows and interdigitate with the orbicularis oculi. They are not attached to the superior temporal line.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis originate from skin of eyebrows

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Orbicularis oris originates from:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle originates from the modiolus (a fibromuscular condensation at the angle of the mouth) and inserts into the lips. It acts as the sphincter of the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris originates from the modiolus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Facial artery:
options: Is a branch of internal carotid artery.
Enters face at antero-inferior angle of Buccinator.
Ends by anastomosing with supraorbital artery.
questions.explanation: The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. It has a tortuous course to accommodate jaw movements and ends at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery has a tortuous course and anastomoses with ophthalmic branches at the medial eye angle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The main sensory nerve of the lower lip is:
questions.explanation: The mental nerve, a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division, V3), exits through the mental foramen to supply the skin of the lower lip and chin.
questions.keyConcept: Mental nerve (V3) is the main sensory nerve of the lower lip

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards orbicularis oculi muscle, all are true EXCEPT:
options: Its lacrimal part helps drainage of tears.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its orbital part has no bony attachment medially.
Its palpebral part lies in the eyelids.
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi has bony attachments both medially (medial palpebral ligament) and laterally (lateral palpebral raphe). Therefore, the statement that it has no medial bony attachment is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi has bony attachments medially and laterally

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The Occipito-frontalis muscle:
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The frontalis portion inserts into the epicranial aponeurosis.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis elevates the eyebrows

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The sphincter of the lips is the:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle of the lips. The buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oris = sphincter of the lips

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the occipital bellies of occipito-frontalis, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: They are separated by an extension of epicranial aponeurosis.
They take origin from epicranial aponeurosis.
They are inserted into lateral 2/3 of highest nuchal line.
They are supplied by temporal branch of facial nerve.
questions.explanation: The two occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis are separated by the median tendinous intersection and take origin from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital bellies originate from the highest nuchal line

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In adults, the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically terminates at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). In neonates, it ends at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Adult spinal cord ends at L1; neonatal spinal cord ends at L3

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In adults the spinal cord usually terminates at the:
options: Upper border of the 12th thoracic vertebra.
Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 4th lumbar vertebra.
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically ends at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is important clinically to avoid spinal cord injury during lumbar puncture, which is performed below this level.
questions.keyConcept: Adult conus medullaris ends at lower border of L1

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced:
options: Below or above tip of 4th L spine.
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1–L2 in adults) to avoid cord injury. The needle is typically introduced at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5 to avoid conus medullaris

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the nuclei of the anterior horn of the spinal cord, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: Its alpha neurons supply intrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anteromedial nucleus extends in all levels of spinal cord.
Its medial nuclear group supply muscles of limbs.
Its gamma neurons supply extrafusal muscle fibers.
Its anterolateral nucleus supplies muscles of hands & feet.
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nuclear group extends at all levels of the spinal cord and supplies the axial muscles. Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal fibers; gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal fibers. The medial group supplies axial muscles, while the lateral group supplies limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anteromedial nucleus extends at all cord levels and supplies axial muscles

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The left spinal lemniscus carries sensations of:
options: Pain from the left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from the left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of the body.
Crude touch from the right side of the body.
Fine touch from right side of body.
questions.explanation: The left spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature from the right side of the body (after decussation). Fine touch and proprioception use the medial lemniscus, not the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus carries contralateral crude sensation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The medial most fibers of the gracile tract are:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract carries sensations from the lower body. Sacral fibers are most medial (closest to the midline), while cervical fibers are most lateral in this tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers are most medial in gracile tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A lesion in the right gracile tract leads to loss of:
options: Sense of position of left big toe.
Sense of movement of right elbow joint.
Feeling of a pencil put in the right hand.
Site of touch on the right iliac fossa.
questions.explanation: A lesion in the right gracile tract affects proprioception and fine touch from the right lower limb. Vibration sense testing of the right tibia would be diminished because this tract carries vibration sense.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion affects ipsilateral lower limb vibration

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient suffered UMNL paralysis in the left lower limb with loss of vibration sense in the same limb and loss of pain sensation in the right lower limb; the most-likely lesion is:
options: Complete transaction of the spinal cord below TI.
Left hemisection of the spinal cord.
Right hemisection of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: Right hemisection (Brown-Sequard): ipsilateral UMNL paralysis, ipsilateral loss of vibration/position sense, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature starting one level below. The description matches right hemisection.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Injury to the right paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The right paracentral lobule controls the left leg. Since motor pathways cross (decussate), injury to the right paracentral lobule causes paralysis of the contralateral (left) lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Right paracentral lobule controls left leg

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following is not a content of the interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a space between the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the oculomotor nerve, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, posterior perforated substance, and cerebral peduncles. The anterior perforated substance is lateral to the optic tract, not in the interpeduncular fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior perforated substance not in interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column (GVA & SVA)?
questions.explanation: Special visceral afferent nuclei receive taste sensation. The nucleus solitarius (particularly its gustatory part) receives taste fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral afferent - taste fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is attached to the malleus and is derived from the mesoderm of the:
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle is derived from mesoderm of the first branchial arch, specifically the first arch mesoderm. It is innervated by the mandibular nerve (CN V3) and attaches to the malleus to dampen sound vibrations. The pre-otic and occipital somites give axial muscles, not branchial arch muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor tympani derived from 1st arch mesoderm; innervated by CN V3; attaches to malleus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Each of the following cells is derived from the neuroepithelial cells EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS and are derived from MONOCYTES (mesodermal origin), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. Neuroepithelial cells give rise to ependymal cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (all neuroglia), and motor neurons. Microglia are unique among CNS cells in being mesodermal in origin.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocytes), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. All other glial cells and neurons come from neuroepithelial cells.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The spinal cord in newly born infant reaches the level of:
questions.explanation: In the newborn infant, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris (end of spinal cord) reaches L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar punctures—needle insertion below L3 avoids spinal cord injury in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord in newborn reaches L3 vertebra; in adults it ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament is called:
questions.explanation: The membrana tectoria is the upward extension of the posterior longitudinal ligament that covers the dens and cruciate ligaments of the atlas. It extends from the body of the axis to the basiocciput, covering the odontoid process. The alar ligaments connect the dens to the occipital condyles; the apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
questions.keyConcept: Membrana tectoria = upward extension of posterior longitudinal ligament covering dens and cruciate ligaments; covers C1-C2 joint.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The structure attached to the side of the odontoid process of the axis vertebra is the:
questions.explanation: The alar ligaments are a pair of strong ligaments attached to the sides of the odontoid process (dens) of the axis vertebra. They connect the dens to the occipital condyles and limit rotation of the head. The apical ligament connects the tip of the dens to the anterior rim of the foramen magnum; the transverse ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas.
questions.keyConcept: Alar ligaments attach to SIDES of odontoid process and connect to occipital condyles; limit head rotation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The type of the atlanto-occipital joint is:
questions.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint is a CONDYLAR (ellipsoid) joint that allows nodding (flexion and extension) and lateral bending. It does NOT allow rotation—this movement occurs at the atlanto-axial joints. The atlanto-occipital joints are synovial joints with articular capsules reinforced by anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Atlanto-occipital joint is CONDYLAR (ellipsoid); allows flexion/extension and lateral bending, NOT rotation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The median atlanto-axial joint:
options: Has the apical ligament connecting dens to atlas.
questions.explanation: The median atlanto-axial joint is a PIVOT (trochoid) joint that allows rotation of the head (turning the head from side to side). This is the key movement tested in the question. The lateral atlanto-axial joints are also pivot joints. The atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid and allows nodding. The apical ligament connects the dens to the anterior foramen magnum.
questions.keyConcept: Median atlanto-axial joint is PIVOT type; allows head rotation. Atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid; allows nodding.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: During a normal child delivery, the attending physician noticed a swelling at the back of a newly born infant, giving a suspicious look for a birth defect. An urgent MRI was requested to assess the structure of the spinal cord. Where should u expect the spinal cord to end in this infant
questions.explanation: In a newborn, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because the vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris ends at L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar puncture, epidural anesthesia, and avoiding spinal cord injury. This infant's spinal cord would end at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord ends at L3 in newborns; by adulthood it ends at L1-L2. Vertebral column grows faster than spinal cord.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which part of the intestine can protrude through a wound just above the umbilicus and to the left?
questions.explanation: The jejunum is the correct answer because wounds above the umbilicus to the left expose the left upper quadrant where coils of jejunum are located. The jejunum begins at the duodenojejunal flexure (at L2 level, left of the midline) and occupies the left upper abdomen. The transverse colon is more centrally located at the umbilical level, sigmoid colon is in the lower left pelvis, and ileum is predominantly in the right lower abdomen and pelvis. Jejunal hernias through abdominal wall defects are clinically recognized due to the fixed mesenteric attachment at the duodenojejunal junction.
questions.keyConcept: The jejunum occupies the left upper abdomen and can protrude through左侧上腹部的伤口.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The main sensory nerve to the lower lip is the:
questions.explanation: The main sensory nerve to the lower lip is the mental nerve (branch of inferior alveolar nerve, which is from V3).选项C正确. The answer is C. It exits via mental foramen.
questions.keyConcept: Mental nerve (V3) is the main sensory nerve to the lower lip - exits at mental foramen.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The roots of the brachial plexus pass between:
questions.explanation: The roots of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) pass between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius muscles. This anatomical relationship is clinically important for thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Brachial plexus roots emerge between anterior and middle scalene muscles before forming trunks.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the first visual area (17):
options: Lies above and below the post calcarine sulcus
Is supplied by posterior cerebral artery
Its lesion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia
All of the above is true
questions.explanation: All statements about visual area 17 are true: it lies on both banks of the calcarine sulcus, extends onto the occipital pole, is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, and lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: Primary visual cortex (V1): straddles calcarine sulcus, supplied by PCA, lesions cause contralateral visual field defects.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The vein that opens in the straight sinus is:
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) receives internal cerebral veins and drains into the straight sinus; internal cerebral vein drains deep structures into great cerebral vein.
questions.keyConcept: Straight sinus drainage

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has a lesion affecting the right gracile tract. Which of the following sensory deficits is most likely?
options: Pain and temperature loss in the right tibia
Vibration loss in the right tibia
Pain and temperature loss in the left tibia
Vibration loss in the left tibia
Complete loss of all sensations in both legs
questions.explanation: Gracile tract lesion causes loss of vibration and proprioception from the ipsilateral lower limb below the midthigh, as the gracile nucleus receives input from the leg and lower trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract carries ipsilateral lower limb proprioceptive information to the medulla.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which type of fibers are carried by the Edinger-Westphal nucleus?
questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus contains preganglionic parasympathetic (visceral efferent) fibers that travel with the oculomotor nerve (III) to the ciliary ganglion, innervating the ciliary and pupillary sphincter muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic fibers to intraocular muscles via CN III.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tissue layer contains arteries, veins, and nerves forming the neurovascular plane?
questions.explanation: The superficial fascia (hypodermis) contains arteries, veins, and nerves forming the neurovascular supply to the skin. It lies between the dermis and deep fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial fascia is the layer containing cutaneous neurovascular bundles between skin and deep fascia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nerve group cell with different origin , function:
questions.explanation: A fasciculus is a compact bundle of fibers having different origins and functions but traveling together, such as the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
questions.keyConcept: Fasciculus definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterior column is ........ while lateral, anterior is............
questions.explanation: The posterior column carries only ascending (sensory) fibers, while both lateral and anterior columns contain mixed ascending and descending fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal column fiber types

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Central canal in CNS is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal of the CNS is lined by simple cuboidal epithelial cells (ependymal cells), which also line the ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal lining

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which Nuclei is present in lateral horn?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic (intermediolateral) nucleus is present in the lateral horn at T1-L2 levels, containing preganglionic sympathetic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sympathetic Nuclei is present in:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn from thoracic to upper 2 lumbar segments (T1-L2).
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic outflow

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior column is present between:
questions.explanation: The anterior column is located between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neuron pools.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior column boundaries

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of proprioception pathway except:
options: large cell in spinal ganglia, thick unmyleinated nerve fiber
enter CNS from medial division of posterior column of white matter
medium cell in spinal ganglia, thin unmyleinated fiber
long ascending as Gracile , cuneate tract
questions.explanation: Proprioception uses large cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia and thick myelinated fibers, not medium cells with thin unmyelinated fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception pathway characteristics

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Gracile tract arise from:
questions.explanation: The gracile fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower body (sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cuneate tract arise from:
questions.explanation: The cuneate fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the upper body (cervical and upper thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Gracile, cuneate tract are:
options: may be same or opposite side
questions.explanation: Gracile and cuneate tracts ascend ipsilaterally in the posterior columns before crossing in the medulla at the sensory decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior column laterality

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of crude touch except:
options: medium sized cell in spinal ganglia
enter medial division of posterior root
small sized cell in spinal ganglia
questions.explanation: Crude touch uses medium-sized cells in dorsal root ganglia (not small), entering via the medial division of the posterior root, and ends in cortex area 3,1,2.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch pathway

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: First order neuron in crude touch end in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons for crude touch have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia; their central processes enter the posterior root and ascend in the posterior column.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch first neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: First order neuron of pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
options: small cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
small cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root
medium cell in spinal ganglia, lateral division of posterior root
large cell in spinal ganglia, medial division of posterior root
questions.explanation: First order neurons for pain/temperature are small cells in dorsal root ganglia whose fibers enter via the lateral division of the posterior root and synapse in substantia gelatinosa.
questions.keyConcept: Pain first order neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The first order neuron in proprioception from the upper half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in proprioception from the upper body also have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia), same as lower body.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first neuron upper body

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal arcuate fibres:
options: Arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Terminate at gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Carry proprioceptive impulses from the head.
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the medulla, cross at the sensory decussation, and form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Origin of medial lemniscus is:
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of same side.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of opposite side.
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus originates from the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side after their fibers cross (internal arcuate fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following is true about first order neurons in proprioception of the body:
options: They are the small cells in spinal ganglia.
They have thin unmyelinated nerve fibres.
Their central branches enter the spinal cord through the lateral division of the posterior roots.
They give ascending and descending branches in spinal cord.
questions.explanation: First order proprioceptive neurons have large cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia with thick myelinated fibers that give off ascending and descending branches in the posterior column.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with lesion in the right gracile nucleus is expected to have diminished:
options: tactile localization at the right arm
fine touch at the left leg
tactile discrimination at the right leg
questions.explanation: Lesion of the right gracile nucleus impairs fine touch and stereognosis on the right lower limb (ipsilateral) because the gracile tract is already ipsilateral.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile nucleus lesion effects

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following structures is a content of interpeduncular fossa:
questions.explanation: The optic tract is a content of the interpeduncular fossa, carrying visual information from the optic chiasma to the lateral geniculate body.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa contents

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The neurologist observes a patient with a high stamping gait. He asks the patient to stand and to close his eyes. The patient immediately starts to sway over. Name the ascending pathways that are involved and name the disease.
options: Gracile on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on one side – Tabes dorsalis.
Gracile on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.
Cuneate on both sides – Tabes dorsalis.
questions.explanation: Bilateral gracile tract degeneration in tabes dorsalis causes loss of proprioception leading to sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign (swaying with eyes closed).
questions.keyConcept: Tabes dorsalis pathology

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The internal arcuate fibres are axons of which nucleus?
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of the cuneate and gracile nuclei that cross at the sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fiber origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: An important virulence factor of *Cryptococcus neoformans* is the production of:
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans produces melanin via phenol oxidase, which protects against oxidative stress and is a major virulence factor.
questions.keyConcept: Cryptococcus virulence

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which characteristic is true of *Listeria monocytogenes*?
options: It is strictly a human pathogen.
It can grow at refrigerator temperature (4°C).
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a psychrophile that can grow at refrigerator temperatures (4°C), enabling it to contaminate refrigerated foods.
questions.keyConcept: Listeria cold tolerance

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In the urea cycle, which two compounds are end products (released from the cycle)?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle products

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which enzyme is stimulated by cortisol to increase epinephrine synthesis?
questions.explanation: PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by cortisol in the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT epinephrine synthesis

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cofactor is required for the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine; BH4 deficiency causes PKU.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The inborn error of branched‑chain amino acid metabolism that causes a burnt‑sugar odour in urine is:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine with characteristic sweet odor.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD biochemistry

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a coenzyme for the oxidative decarboxylation of:
questions.explanation: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids including pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain ketoacids.
questions.keyConcept: TPP coenzyme function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death) is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (B3) deficiency, classically presenting with the 4 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra deficiency

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which vitamin is directly involved in one‑carbon transfer reactions (e.g., purine and thymidylate synthesis)?
questions.explanation: Folate (as N5, N10-methylene-THF) donates one-carbon units in purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Folate one-carbon transfer

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Methyl‑THF donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form:
questions.explanation: Methyl-THF transfers its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
questions.keyConcept: Methyl-THF function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following releases free ammonia in the body?
questions.explanation: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia production

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Glutamate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP are allosteric activators of glutamate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase regulation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is activated by:
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate) is the essential allosteric activator of CPS I, the first urea cycle enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I activation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which compound links the urea cycle with the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: Fumarate links the urea and citric acid cycles; it is produced from argininosuccinate in the urea cycle and enters the CAC.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle CAC link

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Serotonin is synthesised from which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis precursor

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The central nervous system is soft because it:
questions.explanation: The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: CNS softness cause

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The pterion is a clinically important landmark because it overlies the:
options: Anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
questions.explanation: The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery, making it a critical landmark as fractures here can cause epidural hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A lesion of the left optic tract causes:
questions.explanation: A left optic tract lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia because optic tract fibers carry information from the contralateral visual field, so damage affects the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Left optic tract lesion: right homonymous hemianopia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the spinal cord at levels:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from T1 to L2 levels, representing the thoracolumbar outflow of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons: T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The motor branch to mylohyoid arises from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve as the:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives the (motor) nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Motor branch to mylohyoid arises from posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Skin of the hairy area of the temple is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) supplies the hairy temple area, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular division.
questions.keyConcept: Hairy temple: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The common facial vein drains into the ……… vein.
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein after forming from the facial and anterior facial veins joining.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein: drains into internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: An active muscle during whistling is:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle compresses and purses the lips during whistling, while buccinator muscle keeps food between teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Whistling: orbicularis oris contracts to purse lips.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth denotes weakness of ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: Buccinator weakness causes food accumulation in the vestibule because this muscle normally keeps food between the teeth during mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Food in vestibule: buccinator weakness.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following are tributaries of external jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The subclavian artery is divided into 3 parts by ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Pain from upper canine teeth is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The upper canine teeth are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of infraorbital nerve, V2), which also supplies the upper incisors.
questions.keyConcept: Upper canine: anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Choose the wrong statement about the subclavian vein:
options: It is the continuation of the axillary vein.
It is separated from subclavian artery by anterior scalene muscle.
It grooves the 1st rib posterior to scalene tubercle.
It receives the external jugular vein.
questions.explanation: The subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to the anterior scalene muscle (not posterior), making it vulnerable to compression during clavicle fractures.
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to anterior scalene.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Rotation of the head to say "No" occurs at ……… joint.
questions.explanation: Saying 'No' involves rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2), where the dens of the axis articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.
questions.keyConcept: Saying no: rotation at atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A muscle develops from the pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: second pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: First neuron for proprioception from muscles of mastication is:
questions.explanation: The posterior columns (gracile and cuneate nuclei) are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and vertebral arteries, NOT by the anterior spinal artery. The anterior spinal supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior columns not supplied by anterior spinal artery

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Special visceral efferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent nuclei include: trigeminal motor nucleus (V), facial motor nucleus (VII), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI), and hypoglossal nucleus (XII).选项D正确. The answer is D. These innervate pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Special visceral efferent nuclei: CN V, VII, IX, X, XI motor nuclei - innervate pharyngeal arch muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The thalamic nucleus in which spinal & medial lemnisci terminate is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus is the thalamic relay for somatosensory information from the body. Both the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch and proprioception from the body) and the spinal lemniscus (carrying pain and temperature from the body) terminate in the VPL nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VPL nucleus is where spinal lemniscus (pain/temp from body) and medial lemniscus (touch/proprioception from body) terminate.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal carotid blood is lost in injury of the:
questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via branches of the ophthalmic artery. Injury to the forehead region would lead to blood loss from the internal carotid system. The chin and cheek are supplied by external carotid branches.
questions.keyConcept: Forehead injury can lead to internal carotid blood loss

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following arteries does not share in formation of circle of Willis:
questions.explanation: Middle cerebral artery does NOT directly participate in the circle of Willis; it arises from the internal carotid as a branch outside the circle. The circle includes ACA, PCA, ICA, and posterior communicating arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis exclusion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which artery is connected to the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) by the posterior communicating artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior communicating artery (PCoM) connects the internal carotid artery (ICA) with the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), forming part of the circle of Willis and providing collateral circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior communicating artery links ICA to PCA as part of the circle of Willis.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A branch from the internal carotid artery is:
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is a crucial branch of the internal carotid artery as it emerges from the cavernous part, supplying the eye and orbital structures.
questions.keyConcept: Internal carotid branch: ophthalmic artery.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Intermediolateral group of neurons is in:
questions.explanation: The intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) contains the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons and is located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord gray matter (T1–L2).
questions.keyConcept: Intermediolateral cell column = lateral horn = sympathetic preganglionic neurons

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (SCSG) gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
options: Communicating branches with last 4 cranial nerves.
A cardiac branch to superficial cardiac plexus.
questions.explanation: The superior cervical sympathetic ganglion is the largest cervical sympathetic ganglion, located at the level of C2-C3. It gives communicating branches to the last four cranial nerves (IX, X, XI, XII), pharyngeal branches for the pharyngeal plexus, cardiac branches to the superficial cardiac plexus, superior laryngeal nerve fibers, and external and internal carotid plexuses. It does NOT give direct tracheal branches (these come from the middle and inferior ganglia).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion does NOT give tracheal branches.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Inability to recognize familiar objects by touch indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) results from lesions in the superior parietal lobule, which integrates sensory information for object recognition.
questions.keyConcept: Astereognosis: superior parietal lobule lesion.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Conversion of Phenylalanine to tyrosine is catalyzed by phenylalanine hydroxylase which requires.
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, along with oxygen and NADPH. BH4 is also required for tyrosine hydroxylase (dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin synthesis).
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: requires BH4, O2, NADPH. BH4 deficiency causes malignant PKU.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Urea cycle is a pathway that
options: takes place mainly in the liver cells.
questions.explanation: The urea cycle occurs exclusively in the liver (hepatocytes) and is the body's mechanism for converting toxic ammonia (NH3) into urea for excretion. It does not produce ammonia from urea; that would be the reverse reaction which does not occur physiologically.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle location in liver and its role in ammonia detoxification

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which amino acids are responsible for the characteristic burned sugar odor of urine in maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate in maple syrup urine disease due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Hyper-homocysteinemia may result from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of pyridoxine (B6, needed for transsulfuration to cysteine), cobalamin (B12, needed for remethylation to methionine), or folic acid (needed for the folate cycle that donates methyl groups).
questions.keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia: B6, B12, or folate deficiency → elevated homocysteine → cardiovascular risk, neurological issues.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Two reactions of the urea cycle take place in the mitochondria. These are
options: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamoylase.
questions.explanation: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in mitochondria: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate, and ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine. The remaining reactions occur in the cytosol.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial steps of urea cycle: CPS I and OTC

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Asparagine is important as
options: an intermediate of the urea cycle.
an aminoacid that is formed by post-translational modification.
a primary source of ammonia in the kidney.
a requirement for certain cancer cells.
questions.explanation: Asparagine is critical for certain cancers (e.g., acute lymphoblastic leukemia) because they cannot synthesize it (lack asparagine synthetase) and require exogenous asparagine. Asparaginase enzyme therapy depletes circulating asparagine to starve tumor cells.
questions.keyConcept: Asparagine as essential requirement for certain cancer cells (asparaginase therapy)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Uremia occurs in
questions.explanation: Uremia refers to accumulation of urea and other nitrogenous waste products in the blood. In cirrhosis, the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea effectively, leading to elevated blood urea and uremic symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Cirrhosis causes uremia due to impaired hepatic urea synthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The clinical picture of classic phenylketonuria results from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Classic PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine deficiency (tyrosine is an essential dietary requirement in PKU).
questions.keyConcept: PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine scarcity

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about folate requirement?
options: Folic acid requirement is about 300-400 μg/day.
The need for folate nearly doubles by the third trimester of pregnancy.
Folic acid is present primarily in leafy vegetables; in addition to yeast and liver.
questions.explanation: Folate requirement is 300-400 mcg/day, nearly doubles in the third trimester (400-800 mcg), and is present in leafy vegetables, yeast, and liver. All statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Folate: 300-400 mcg/day requirement, doubled in pregnancy, found in leafy vegetables

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which vitamins are directly required for the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine?
questions.explanation: Homocysteine remethylation to methionine requires methyltetrahydrofolate (from folic acid) as methyl donor and methionine synthase (which needs B12).
questions.keyConcept: Homocysteine remethylation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is not adverse effect of Carbamazepine?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia is NOT a carbamazepine adverse effect. Option C is correct. Carbamazepine causes agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, SIADH (dilutional hyponatremia), and is an enzyme inducer. Megaloblastic anemia is associated with phenytoin and valproate (both interfere with folate metabolism).
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes hematologic toxicity (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia) and SIADH, not megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In the same patient (alcoholic, confusion, ataxia), which enzyme is affected?
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; its deficiency impairs this enzyme causing neurological dysfunction in Wernicke-Korsakoff.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine-dependent enzymes

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: N-acetyl-glutamate
options: is an allosteric activator of ornithine transcarbamoylase.
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase. NAG is an obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), and its concentration increases after protein-rich meals when glutamate is abundant.
questions.keyConcept: NAG as allosteric activator of CPS I, increasing postprandially

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (serotonin-secreting tumor) is diagnosed by measuring 5-Hydroxyindole-acetic acid (5-HIAA) in 24-hour urine - this is the main serotonin metabolite. 5-HIAA is elevated in carcinoid tumors. VMA is for pheochromocytoma. Phenylacetylglutamine is a phenylalanine metabolite.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid diagnosis: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite). VMA = catecholamine metabolite (pheochromocytoma).

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following may serve as a tumor marker?
questions.explanation: Both VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and 5-HIAA can serve as tumor markers - VMA for neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma, and 5-HIAA for carcinoid tumors. Phenylpyruvic acid is not a tumor marker.
questions.keyConcept: Tumor markers: VMA (neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma), 5-HIAA (carcinoid). Both can be measured.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes is Important for synthesis of both epinephrine and melatonin?
questions.explanation: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AAAD) converts 5-HTP to serotonin (for melatonin synthesis) and DOPA to dopamine (for epinephrine synthesis). This enzyme is required for both pathways, making it the shared enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: AAAD: converts 5-HTP→serotonin (→melatonin) and DOPA→dopamine (→norepinephrine→epinephrine).

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Catecholamines
questions.explanation: Catecholamines include dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. They function both as neurotransmitters (in the CNS and autonomic nervous system) and as hormones (epinephrine from adrenal medulla). Both statements (a) and (b) are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines (dopamine, NE, E): both neurotransmitters and hormones. Synthesized from tyrosine.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: All of the following are ketogenic Amino acids except:
questions.explanation: Glycine is a glucogenic amino acid, not ketogenic. Leucine and isoleucine are purely ketogenic. Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Lysine is also purely ketogenic. Glycine is converted to serine (glucogenic) or to porphyrins.
questions.keyConcept: Purely ketogenic: leucine, lysine. Both glucogenic/ketogenic: isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan. Glucogenic: glycine, alanine, serine.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The main sites for oxidative deamination are:
questions.explanation: Oxidative deamination (conversion of amino acids to keto acids with release of ammonia) occurs mainly in the LIVER and KIDNEY. These organs have the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase. Other tissues lack significant oxidative deamination capacity.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidative deamination: liver and kidney (glutamate dehydrogenase). Produces ammonia for urea cycle.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The urea cycle is active in cases of
questions.explanation: The urea cycle is active during protein intake (to excrete excess nitrogen) and during fasting (when protein breakdown increases to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis). Both conditions increase nitrogen waste that must be excreted as urea.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle: active during high protein intake and fasting (increased amino acid catabolism).

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in man is:
questions.explanation: Urea is the major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in humans, produced exclusively in the liver via the urea cycle. It is excreted by the kidneys. Ammonia is toxic and must be converted to urea. Uric acid is from purine metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Major nitrogen waste product: urea (from hepatic urea cycle). Ammonia is converted to urea.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: If there were complete absence of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, what would be the source of urea in the blood?
questions.explanation: With CPS-I deficiency, urea cannot be synthesized via the cycle. However, some urea is produced by bacterial action on ammonia in the gut (bacterial urease). The liver's arginase cannot produce urea without upstream cycle intermediates.
questions.keyConcept: CPS-I deficiency: some urea from bacterial urease in intestine, not from hepatic urea cycle.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: N-acetyl glutamate is an essential allosteric activator of:
questions.explanation: N-acetyl glutamate (NAG) is an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I), the first enzyme of the urea cycle in mitochondria. NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase.
questions.keyConcept: N-acetylglutamate: allosteric activator of CPS-I (first urea cycle enzyme). Synthesized from acetyl-CoA + glutamate.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following increases with deficiency of any enzyme of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: When any urea cycle enzyme is deficient, ammonia cannot be efficiently converted to urea. Glutamine synthesis (via glutamine synthetase) increases as an alternative ammonia detoxification pathway, so glutamine levels increase.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle deficiency: increased glutamine (alternative ammonia detoxification). Citrulline may decrease.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following may be true about the glutamine synthetase reaction in the brain?
options: At high ammonia concentration, it can deplete glutamate, with consequent decrease of GABA.
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase in astrocytes converts glutamate + ammonia → glutamine. This normally detoxifies ammonia. At high ammonia, glutamate gets depleted, reducing GABA synthesis (since GABA is made from glutamate), causing neurological symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glutamine synthetase: detoxifies ammonia; depletes glutamate → reduced GABA → neurological dysfunction.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of GLUTAMINE (via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes). The brain uses this pathway to detoxify ammonia. Alanine synthesis occurs in liver (not brain). Glutamate is made from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia but requires different enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Normal ammonia disposal in brain: glutamine synthetase (astrocytes) converts glutamate + NH3 → glutamine.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ammonia toxicity to the brain is Probably through which of the Following mechanisms?
options: Inhibition of energy production in brain Cells.
Production of increased amounts of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
Acidifying effect on the intra- and extracellular fluids.
Conversion to urea, increasing the Osmotic pressure.
Inability of the brain cells to utilize any of the amino acids.
questions.explanation: Ammonia toxicity primarily inhibits the citric acid cycle (energy production) by depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate. It does NOT increase GABA (it decreases it). It causes alkalosis (not acidosis). Brain can still use amino acids.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibits TCA cycle (depletes alpha-ketoglutarate), depletes glutamate → decreased GABA → neurological symptoms.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Hyperammonemia may be caused by
options: genetic defect of any enzyme of urea cycle (primary hyperammonemia).
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia results from genetic defects in any urea cycle enzyme. Secondary hyperammonemia results from liver failure (inability to convert ammonia to urea). Both causes lead to ammonia accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia: primary (urea cycle enzyme defect) or secondary (liver failure). Both cause ammonia accumulation.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The symptom of ammonia intoxication includes.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication primarily affects the brain, causing mental confusion, asterixis (liver flap), and eventually coma. It does not typically cause visual blurring, constipation, or diarrhea as primary symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: brain dysfunction → mental confusion, asterixis, coma. Does not cause GI symptoms primarily.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia Levels are.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia levels are INCREASED (elevated). Normal brain ammonia is kept very low by glutamine synthesis and urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: occurs when brain ammonia levels are elevated, disrupting glutamate/GABA metabolism.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Primary hyperammonemia may be treated by
options: agents that increase excretion of Conjugated amino acids, e.g., benzoic acid and phenylacetate.
acidification of the intestinal lumen to help get rid of ammonia as ammonium Ions.
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia (urea cycle defects) is treated with: low-protein diet (reduce nitrogen load), benzoic acid/phenylacetate (alternative nitrogen excretion as conjugated amino acids), and acidification of intestinal lumen (to trap ammonia as NH4+ for excretion).
questions.keyConcept: Primary hyperammonemia treatment: low protein, alternative nitrogen excretion (benzoic acid, phenylacetate), gut ammonia trapping.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Maple syrup urine disease is an inborn error of metabolism of:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease involves defective metabolism of BRANCHED CHAIN AMINO ACIDS (leucine, isoleucine, valine) due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Accumulated metabolites give urine a maple syrup odor.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease: branched-chain amino acid metabolism defect (BCKDH deficiency).

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of
options: Conversion of phenylalanine to  a phenylketoacid.
Production of phenylalanine from  a phenylketoacid.
Reaction of phenylalanine with an α-ketoacid.
Conversion of phenylalanine to another aminoacid.
questions.explanation: PKU results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency prevents the normal metabolism of phenylalanine, leading to accumulation and conversion to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate).
questions.keyConcept: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones → intellectual disability if untreated.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The major contributor to the one-carbon pool?
questions.explanation: Serine is the major contributor to the one-carbon pool through its conversion to glycine, releasing a methylene group (-CH2-). The methyl group can be transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming N5,N10-methylene-THF.
questions.keyConcept: One-carbon pool: serine → glycine transfers CH2 to THF. Also from histidine, tryptophan, methionine.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Methionine is synthesized in human body from:
questions.explanation: Methionine is synthesized from homocysteine and serine via methionine synthase (requires B12) and other enzymes. The pathway involves converting homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
questions.keyConcept: Methionine synthesis: homocysteine + serine → methionine (requires B12, folate). Cysteine is made from serine + homocysteine separately.

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is phenylketonuria?
options: A condition caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin reductase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin biosynthesis
A condition caused by a deficiency of homocystinuria
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
questions.keyConcept: PKU phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What are the clinical pictures of phenylketonuria?
options: Urine with a bad mousy odor
questions.explanation: PKU clinical features include intellectual disability (if untreated), hypopigmentation (decreased tyrosine reduces melanin), and characteristic mousy/musty odor from phenylacetate accumulation in urine and sweat.
questions.keyConcept: PKU clinical manifestations

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: How is phenylketonuria treated?
options: A diet low in phenylalanine, supplementation of tyrosine
Giving DOPA and serotonin if there is dihydrobiopterin deficiency
questions.explanation: PKU treatment involves lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction with tyrosine supplementation (since tyrosine becomes essential); with defective BH4 metabolism, DOPA and 5-HTP supplementation is also required.
questions.keyConcept: PKU dietary and pharmacological treatment

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is maple syrup urine disease?
options: A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in phenylalanine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tyrosine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tryptophan catabolism
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and their ketoacids.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain dehydrogenase deficiency

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What are the effects of maple syrup urine disease?
options: Mental retardation and may lead to early death
The urine has a sweet smell-like maple syrup or burned sugar
questions.explanation: MSUD manifests as mental retardation, developmental delay, feeding difficulties, and characteristic sweet maple syrup/burnt sugar odor of urine from accumulating branched-chain ketoacids; untreated cases often fatal in infancy.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD clinical presentation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is the treatment for maple syrup urine disease?
options: A diet low in branched-chain amino acids
questions.explanation: MSUD treatment requires lifelong restriction of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in diet, with careful monitoring of amino acid levels to prevent neurological damage.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain amino acid restriction

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In fasting conditions, glucose is provided for the brain by
questions.explanation: In fasting, brain glucose comes from hepatic glycogenolysis (immediately) and gluconeogenesis from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol (sustained); intestine is not a source during fasting.
questions.keyConcept: Fasting brain glucose sources

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Brain cells oxidize glucose to
questions.explanation: Brain cells completely oxidize glucose to CO2 and H2O via aerobic metabolism in mitochondria, producing 30-32 ATP per glucose molecule.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glucose complete oxidation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In brain cells, glucose is phosphorylated by
questions.explanation: Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.
questions.keyConcept: Brain hexokinase glucose phosphorylation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Glucose 6-phosphate is utilized in which pathway in brain cells?
questions.explanation: Glucose 6-phosphate in brain cells enters glycolysis; the pentose phosphate pathway also operates for nucleotide synthesis, but glycolysis is the main utilization pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Brain G6P glycolysis pathway

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is the importance of HMP pathway in the brain cells?
questions.explanation: HMP pathway's main importance in brain is generating NADPH for antioxidant defense (via glutathione reductase) and nucleotide synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: HMP pathway brain antioxidant role

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Hormones and neurotransmitters
options: are signal molecules used for cell-cell communication.
are mostly polypeptides or nitrogenous compounds, both derived from amino-acids.
questions.explanation: Hormones and neurotransmitters are signal molecules for cell-cell communication, derived from amino acids (nitrogenous) but also include non-nitrogenous compounds like steroid hormones.
questions.keyConcept: Signal molecules characteristics

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following aminoacids may act as a neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are all amino acid neurotransmitters; glycine and GABA are inhibitory, glutamate is excitatory.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid neurotransmitters

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA) is produced by
options: a reaction that requires vitamin B6 derived cofactor.
questions.explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), requiring PLP (vitamin B6) as cofactor; both a and c are correct.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis glutamate decarboxylase

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the aminoacid neurotransmitters?
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen aminoacids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other aminoacids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
questions.explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate is excitatory, glycine/GABA are inhibitory; glycine is in collagen; glutamate produces MSG; all above is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid NT properties

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: L-Dopa (Dihydroxyphenylalanine) is
options: converted to tyrosine by a hydroxylase enzyme.
questions.explanation: L-DOPA is produced from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase (not from dopamine); dopamine is synthesized from L-DOPA by DOPA decarboxylase. Option D (neither) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: L-DOPA synthesis pathway

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis is
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step by hydroxylating tyrosine to form DOPA; both formation of DOPA and hydroxylation of tyrosine describe the same step.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase rate limiting

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Norepinephrine is produced by
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is synthesized from dopamine via hydroxylation by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, which requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and copper as a cofactor. This is the primary pathway for norepinephrine production in the adrenal medulla and CNS neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine synthesis pathway and dopamine beta-hydroxylase reaction

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Production of norepinephrine from dopamine requires
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. This enzyme is a copper-containing monooxygenase that requires vitamin C as an electron donor and tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. Both cofactors are essential for activity, hence answer D.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase cofactors: copper, vitamin C, and tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Production of epinephrine from nor-epinephrine requires
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized from norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. PNMT is expressed primarily in the adrenal medulla. The combination of PNMT enzyme and SAM availability makes both factors necessary.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine using SAM as methyl donor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Catecholamines are catabolized by
options: monoamine oxidase (MAO), followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are catabolized by both MAO (monoamine oxidase) and COMT (catechol O-methyltransferase), acting sequentially or independently. MAO acts first in mitochondria, followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase; COMT O-methylates catecholamines directly. Both pathways contribute to VMA production.
questions.keyConcept: Dual catabolism of catecholamines by MAO and COMT pathways

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is
questions.explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action on catecholamines, then further metabolism to VMA. Elevated VMA is a key diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA as the end product of catecholamine catabolism and tumor marker

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan results in formation of
questions.explanation: 5-hydroxytryptophan is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) to form serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan via decarboxylation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Serotonin is
options: produced by N-acetylation and O-methylation of melatonin.
questions.explanation: Serotonin is chemically 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan. It is not a tyrosine derivative (that would be catecholamines); rather, it is an indoleamine derived from tryptophan. Melatonin is formed from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation, not the reverse.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin (5-HT) as an indoleamine, not a catecholamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Serotonin is catabolized by
questions.explanation: Serotonin is catabolized primarily by monoamine oxidase (MAO), which oxidatively deaminates it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, further converted to 5-HIAA. COMT does not significantly metabolize serotonin since it is not a catecholamine.
questions.keyConcept: MAO as the primary catabolic enzyme for serotonin

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following increases in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)?
