questions.explanation: In pheochromocytoma, excess catecholamines are secreted and metabolized, producing elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is the end product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine catabolism and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: VMA elevation in urine as diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Histamine is formed from histidine by
options: a reaction that requires pyridoxal phosphate.
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine, and this enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase also participates in histamine metabolism in some contexts, requiring the same cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine synthesis from histidine requiring PLP cofactor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Tyramine
options: is the decarboxylation product of tyrosine, which is present in aged food.
can displace catecholamines from their stores.
may precipitate a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors as anti-depressant.
questions.explanation: Tyramine is formed by bacterial decarboxylation of tyrosine in aged foods (cheese, wine). It displaces catecholamines from synaptic vesicles, and in patients on MAO inhibitors, this can cause massive catecholamine release leading to hypertensive crisis (the 'cheese effect').
questions.keyConcept: Tyramine in aged foods and cheese effect with MAO inhibitors

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Nitric oxide is a hormone and a neurotransmitter produced
options: by the action of nitric oxide synthase.
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized from arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), which requires oxygen and NADPH. Glycine is not a precursor for NO; it is involved in purine metabolism and as a neurotransmitter. The NOS reaction also produces citrulline.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthesis from arginine by NOS requiring O2 and NADPH

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Nitric oxide synthase
options: acts on arginine and needs Oxygen and NADPH.
has three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial and phagocytic.
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase exists as three isozymes: neuronal (nNOS), endothelial (eNOS), and phagocytic/inducible (iNOS). All isoforms convert arginine to citrulline and NO using NADPH and oxygen. The reaction produces both citrulline and nitric oxide as products.
questions.keyConcept: Three NOS isoforms: neuronal, endothelial, and phagocytic

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is
questions.explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages.
questions.keyConcept: iNOS as calcium-independent NOS isozyme in phagocytes

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In the urea cycle, urea is produced from
options: carbon dioxide and ammonium ions by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.
questions.explanation: Arginine is cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine in the final step of the urea cycle. Fumarate is produced earlier from argininosuccinate. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase initiates the cycle by fixing ammonia and CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Arginase cleavage of arginine to produce urea and ornithine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Although arginine is formed in the urea cycle, it is considered an essential amino-acid. Why?
options: It must be broken down by arginase enzyme.
Its rate of synthesis is not enough for growing children.
It is formed in the cytosol, therefore it cannot be used.
It is formed in the D-configuration.
questions.explanation: Although the urea cycle synthesizes arginine, the rate of endogenous synthesis is insufficient for the demands of rapid growth in infants and children, making it a conditionally essential amino acid during development. Adults normally synthesize adequate arginine.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as conditionally essential amino acid in children

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is a high energy compound formed in the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate is a high-energy compound formed in the first step of the urea cycle, consuming 2 ATP equivalents. It donates its energy to drive the subsequent reaction. Ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not high-energy compounds.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamoyl phosphate as the high-energy intermediate of urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following aminoacids is formed in the urea cycle and used in protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Arginine is the only urea cycle intermediate that is incorporated into proteins; ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not standard proteinogenic amino acids.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as the only proteinogenic amino acid in urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ornithine is an aminoacid formed from
options: arginine and can be transformed to glutamate in two steps.
glutamate and can be transformed to arginine in the urea cycle.
arginine and transformed to aceto-acetate on fasting.
questions.explanation: Ornithine is produced from arginine by arginase and can be transaminated to glutamate via ornithine aminotransferase. Conversely, glutamate can be converted to ornithine through acetylation (N-acetylglutamate) and subsequent reactions in the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Ornithine-glutamate interconversion in nitrogen metabolism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In the urea cycle, which aminoacids should be transported between the mitochondria and the cytosol in either direction?
questions.explanation: Ornithine must be transported from mitochondria to cytosol (where it combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline), and citrulline must travel back to mitochondria for the next step. This mitochondrial-cytosolic transport is essential for urea cycle function.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial-cytosolic transport of ornithine and citrulline

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is produced by the urea cycle with the production of urea?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle produces fumarate when argininosuccinate is cleaved by argininosuccinase. Fumarate can enter the TCA cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Fumarate production from argininosuccinate in urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: How many carbon and nitrogen atoms are there in a urea molecule?
questions.explanation: Urea has the formula (NH2)2C=O, containing ONE carbon atom and TWO nitrogen atoms.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibition of TCA cycle enzymes and glutamate accumulation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is the source of urea carbon?
questions.explanation: The carbon of urea comes from CO2 (as bicarbonate) via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondria.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting enzyme requiring NAG for activation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following gives one nitrogen atom of the urea molecule?
questions.explanation: One nitrogen of urea comes from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase joining citrulline with aspartate's amino group). Glutamate provides nitrogen via transamination, not directly as a source.
questions.keyConcept: Citrullinemia type I from ASS deficiency with citrulline elevation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is a source of urea nitrogen?
questions.explanation: One nitrogen of urea comes from ammonia (via CPS I combining NH3 with CO2 to form carbamoyl phosphate). The second nitrogen comes from aspartate.
questions.keyConcept: OTC deficiency as most common X-linked urea cycle disorder

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Glutamate can be the source of both nitrogen atoms of urea through which reactions?
questions.explanation: Glutamate provides nitrogen via both glutamate dehydrogenase (oxidative deamination releasing NH3) and glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase (transamination to form aspartate for urea cycle).
questions.keyConcept: Glycine cleavage system in mitochondria for glycine catabolism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ammonia is introduced in the urea cycle by
options: reacting as ammonium ion with carbon dioxide and ATP.
making a part of N-acetyl glutamate.
questions.explanation: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes the reversible interconversion of serine and glycine in the cytosol and mitochondria. This reaction transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, essential for nucleotide synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Serine-glycine interconversion via SHMT generating one-carbon units

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: How is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I different from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II?
options: I is mitochondrial while II is cytosolic.
I is used for pyrimidine synthesis but II is for urea synthesis.
I does not need N-acetyl glutamate as allosteric activator, unlike II.
I uses glutamine not ammonia as a nitrogen donor.
questions.explanation: CPS I is mitochondrial and participates in the urea cycle (using ammonia and CO2), while CPS II is cytosolic and involved in pyrimidine synthesis (using glutamine). CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator; CPS II does not.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I (mitochondrial, urea cycle) vs CPS II (cytosolic, pyrimidine synthesis)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is an energy-producing pathway?
questions.explanation: The citrate (Krebs) cycle produces energy by oxidizing acetyl-CoA, generating NADH, FADH2, and GTP. The urea cycle consumes energy (4 ATP equivalents) and does not produce ATP; its purpose is ammonia detoxification.
questions.keyConcept: Citric acid cycle as energy-producing pathway, urea cycle as energy-consuming

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: How many ATP (energy currency) are used in one turn of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: One turn of the urea cycle consumes 4 high-energy phosphate bonds: 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, 1 ATP to form argininosuccinate (AMP + PPi, counting as 2), with fumarate oxidation linking to the TCA cycle to recover some energy.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle energy cost: 4 ATP equivalents per turn

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following reactions linked to urea cycle may help covering its energy cost?
options: Malate dehydrogenase involved in aspartate regeneration from fumarate.
Glutamate dehydrogenase involved in provision of ammonia.
Glutaminase involved in provision of ammonia.
questions.explanation: The fumarate produced in the urea cycle enters the TCA cycle where malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate, which is transaminated back to aspartate (used in argininosuccinate synthesis). Glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase provide ammonia for the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: TCA cycle link to urea cycle via fumarate and aspartate regeneration

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: ATP is consumed in which of the following reactions?
questions.explanation: ATP is consumed in the CPS I reaction (2 ATP to 1 ADP) and the argininosuccinate synthetase reaction (ATP to AMP + PPi, effectively 2 ATP). Ornithine transcarbamylase does not require ATP; it transfers the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine.
questions.keyConcept: ATP consumption at CPS I and ASS steps of urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is the use of glutamate for the urea cycle?
options: Production of ammonia by glutamate dehydrogenase reaction.
Regeneration of aspartate by the glutamate:oxaloacetate transaminase reaction.
Formation of the cycle activator: N-acetyl-glutamate.
questions.explanation: Glutamate serves multiple roles: glutamate dehydrogenase provides ammonia (with NADPH), glutamate:oxaloacetate transaminase regenerates aspartate for argininosuccinate synthesis, and glutamate is the precursor for N-acetylglutamate synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate as central nitrogen donor and NAG precursor for urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: How is citric acid cycle useful for urea cycle?
options: Regeneration of aspartate from fumarate, through malate and oxalo-acetate.
questions.explanation: The TCA cycle generates ATP/GTP and also regenerates aspartate from fumarate through malate and oxaloacetate. Aspartate is required for argininosuccinate formation, linking these cycles. Thus both energy provision and anaplerosis connect them.
questions.keyConcept: TCA cycle support of urea cycle via energy and aspartate regeneration

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is true about urea cycle?
options: Its rate varies with the type of food.
Is not necessary in times of fasting.
The concentration of its enzymes is constant.
It is a closed pathway, with its intermediates not involved in other metabolic reactions.
questions.explanation: The urea cycle rate adapts to dietary protein content: higher protein intake increases amino acid deamination and ammonia production, upregulating urea cycle activity. It operates continuously, even during fasting when muscle protein breakdown releases nitrogen.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle rate variation with dietary protein intake

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which reaction of the urea cycle is the primary control reaction of the pathway?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, controlled allosterically by N-acetylglutamate (NAG). This ensures the cycle activates only when ammonia and acetyl-CoA are available for detoxification.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting, NAG-regulated step of urea cycle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The rate of the urea cycle is controlled by
options: arginine, which activates the synthesis of the allosteric activator.
questions.explanation: Urea cycle rate is regulated at multiple levels: substrate (ammonia) availability stimulates CPS I, enzyme levels increase during high protein intake via induction, and arginine activates N-acetylglutamate synthase to boost CPS I activity.
questions.keyConcept: Multi-level regulation of urea cycle: substrate, induction, and allosteric control

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In fasting conditions, glucose is provided for the brain by:
questions.explanation: In fasting, liver glycogen is depleted within 12-18 hours, after which hepatic gluconeogenesis (from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids) becomes the primary source of glucose for the brain. Intestinal absorption is minimal 6 hours post-meal.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic gluconeogenesis becomes primary glucose source for brain during fasting

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In carcinoid syndrome the argentaffin tissue of the abdominal cavity overproduce:
questions.explanation: In carcinoid syndrome, the argentaffin (enterochromaffin) cells of the gut overproduce serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) from tryptophan. This causes the characteristic symptoms: diarrhea, flushing, and cardiac valvular fibrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid syndrome overproduces serotonin from argentaffin cells

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The rate limiting step in the biosynthesis of catecholamines is:
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA, which is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by catecholamines.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine biosynthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following amine acids may act as a neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are the three major amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS. Glycine is inhibitory in spinal cord; glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter; GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter.
questions.keyConcept: Glycine, glutamate, and GABA as the three major amino acid neurotransmitters

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The enzyme dopamine beta-oxidase (hydroxylase) which catalyzes conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine requires:
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor for the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. The enzyme also contains copper. This is why ascorbate deficiency can impair catecholamine synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as cofactor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Histamine is formed from histidine by:
questions.explanation: Histidine is decarboxylated by histidine decarboxylase to form histamine, analogous to other neurotransmitter synthesis pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: A vasodilating compound is produced by the decarboxylation of the amino acid:
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylation produces histamine, which is a potent vasodilator. Histamine acts on H1 receptors causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylation produces vasodilator histamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA) is produced by:
options: A reaction that requires vitamin B6 derived cofactor.
questions.explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid (glutamate) via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis from glutamate via GAD requiring PLP (B6) cofactor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The defective enzyme in histidinemia is:
questions.explanation: Histidinemia is caused by a deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase), which normally converts histidine to urocanic acid. This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder presenting with intellectual disability and speech defects.
questions.keyConcept: Histidase deficiency causes histidinemia (histidine ammonia-lyase)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Serotonin is synthesized from:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is synthesized from the essential amino acid tryptophan via hydroxylation (tryptophan hydroxylase) to 5-hydroxytryptophan, then decarboxylation to serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesized from tryptophan (not tyrosine or phenylalanine)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following increases in 24 Hour urine with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma secretes excess catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), which are metabolized to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is measured in 24-hour urine as the primary diagnostic marker for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: VMA elevated in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome diagnosis uses elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main serotonin metabolite, not serotonin itself.
questions.keyConcept: 5-HIAA in 24-hour urine is diagnostic for carcinoid syndrome

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the amino acid neurotransmitters?
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while Glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen amino acids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other amino acids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
questions.explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are correct: glutamate is excitatory, glycine and GABA are inhibitory; glycine constitutes one-third of collagen; glutamic acid is produced from other amino acids; monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.
questions.keyConcept: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate excitatory, glycine/GABA inhibitory

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Histamine is formed from histidine by which of the following enzymes or reactions:
options: A reaction that requires pyridoxal phosphate.
questions.explanation: Histamine is formed from histidine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. This reaction is analogous to other decarboxylations in neurotransmitter synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylase (ALAD) requires PLP to form histamine from histidine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Nitric Oxide is a hormone and a neurotransmitter synthesized:
options: By the action of nitric oxide synthase.
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized by nitric oxide synthase from the amino acid arginine (not glycine), producing citrulline and NO. NO acts as a gaseous neurotransmitter and vasodilator.
questions.keyConcept: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine (not glycine) to NO and citrulline

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: GABA (gamma amino butyric acid) is:
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A (ionotropic, chloride channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors. It is produced postsynaptically from glutamate by GAD.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is the major postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in CNS

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Mono Amine Oxidase (MAO) catalyzes the conversion of serotonin to:
questions.explanation: MAO converts serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, which is then oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to 5-HIAA.
questions.keyConcept: MAO converts serotonin to 5-HIAA via aldehyde intermediate

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: L-Dopa (Dihydroxyphenylalanine) is:
options: Converted to tyrosine by a hydroxylase enzyme.
questions.explanation: L-dopa (dihydroxyphenylalanine) is produced by hydroxylation of tyrosine (not decarboxylation of noradrenaline), catalyzed by tyrosine hydroxylase. It is then converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase).
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa formed by tyrosine hydroxylation, not noradrenaline decarboxylation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis is:
questions.explanation: The hydroxylation of tyrosine to DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis. This enzyme requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor and is feedback-inhibited by the end products.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan results in formation of:
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) produces serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
questions.keyConcept: 5-hydroxytryptophan decarboxylation produces serotonin (5-HT)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Serotonin is:
options: Produced by N-acetylation and methylation of melatonin.
questions.explanation: Serotonin is 5-hydroxytryptamine, synthesized from tryptophan (not a tyrosine derivative). Melatonin is produced from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation, not the reverse pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin is 5-HT, an indoleamine from tryptophan, not tyrosine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Serotonin is catabolized by:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is primarily catabolized by monoamine oxidase (MAO), which oxidatively deaminates it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde. This is further oxidized to 5-HIAA. COMT does not significantly metabolize serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: MAO is the primary catabolic enzyme for serotonin

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Vitamin B-derived coenzyme is needed for the synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is converted from L-dopa by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, B6) as a cofactor. PNMT (for epinephrine from norepinephrine) uses SAM; melatonin from serotonin does not require B6-derived cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: ALAD requires PLP (B6) to convert L-dopa to dopamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Melatonin is synthesized from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Melatonin is synthesized from tryptophan via the pathway: tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin to N-acetylserotonin to melatonin.
questions.keyConcept: Melatonin synthesized from tryptophan (not tyrosine, melanin, or MSH)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is a tumor marker that indicates high adrenaline secretion?
questions.explanation: Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the end product of catecholamine catabolism and is elevated in pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA in urine as tumor marker for pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Catecholamines are:
questions.explanation: Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) function both as circulating hormones (from adrenal medulla) and as neurotransmitters (in the CNS and sympathetic nervous system). They contain the catechol ring structure.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines function as both circulating hormones and neurotransmitters

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Regarding the structure of catecholamines:
options: Contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring in their structure.
Are synthesized from the amino acid glycine.
questions.explanation: Catecholamines contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring structure and are synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine, not glycine. The catechol ring is essential for their biological activity.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines contain catechol ring, synthesized from tyrosine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following reactions produces carbon dioxide?
options: Conversion of acetyl CoA to malonyl CoA.
Synthesis of serotonin from its precursor.
Action of monoamine oxidase on norepinephrine.
questions.explanation: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase produces CO2 as a byproduct of the decarboxylation reaction. Acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis) also produces CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Decarboxylation of 5-HTP to serotonin produces carbon dioxide

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is measured in the urine to confirm the presence of an adrenaline secreting tumor?
questions.explanation: Vanillomandelic acid (VMA) in urine confirms pheochromocytoma, as it is the major end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline metabolism. Elevated urinary VMA is a sensitive screening test for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Vanillomandelic acid (VMA) in urine confirms adrenaline-secreting tumor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Norepinephrine is produced by:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is produced by hydroxylation of dopamine via dopamine beta-hydroxylase. This enzyme requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid), copper, and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase hydroxylates dopamine to form norepinephrine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Production of norepinephrine from dopamine requires:
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is a copper-containing oxidase that hydroxylates dopamine to norepinephrine. It requires vitamin C as an electron donor and tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. Both a and b are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires copper, vitamin C, and tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Hormones and neurotransmitters:
options: Are signal molecules used for cell-cell communication.
Are mostly polypeptides or nitrogenous compounds, both derived from amino acids.
questions.explanation: Hormones and neurotransmitters are signal molecules for cell-cell communication, mostly derived from amino acids (polypeptides, nitrogenous compounds). Non-nitrogenous signal molecules (like steroid hormones, fatty acid derivatives) also exist.
questions.keyConcept: Signal molecules include both nitrogenous and non-nitrogenous compounds

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Vitamin B6 is important for which of the following regarding brain metabolism?
options: Detoxification of ammonia by formation of glutamine.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) is essential for synthesizing major neurotransmitters: dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, GABA, and histamine, all produced by PLP-dependent decarboxylation reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B6 (PLP) required for synthesis of major CNS neurotransmitters

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is:
questions.explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA as end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following coenzymes is required for the synthesis of GABA, serotonin, and histamine from their respective amino acid precursors?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6) is the cofactor for decarboxylation reactions that produce GABA, serotonin, and histamine.
questions.keyConcept: PLP (B6) is the common cofactor for GABA, serotonin, and histamine synthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) occurs by a:
questions.explanation: GABA is synthesized by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), which requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. This is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis by PLP-dependent decarboxylation of glutamate

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Production of epinephrine from norepinephrine requires:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized from norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. Both the enzyme and SAM are required.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine using SAM as methyl donor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Catecholamines are catabolized by:
options: Monoamine oxidase (MAO), followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are catabolized by both MAO (followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase) and COMT, acting in sequence or independently. These pathways produce VMA as the final urinary metabolite.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine catabolism by both MAO and COMT pathways

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Nitric oxide synthase:
options: Acts on arginine and needs oxygen and NADPH.
Has three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial and phagocytic.
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase (all three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial, and phagocytic/inducible) converts arginine to citrulline and nitric oxide, requiring oxygen and NADPH as cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: NOS produces NO and citrulline from arginine; three isozymes exist

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is a substrate for nitric oxide synthase?
questions.explanation: Arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase, which converts it to citrulline and nitric oxide. GTP is for guanylyl cyclase; glycine is for porphyrin synthesis; nitric oxide is the product, not substrate.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase to produce NO

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following may be considered a physiological ammonia-fixing reaction?
questions.explanation: Both glutamine synthetase (in brain and peripheral tissues) and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (in liver mitochondria) fix ammonia. Glutamine synthetase incorporates ammonia into glutamine for safe transport; CPS I initiates the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase and CPS I are physiological ammonia-fixing reactions

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Synthesis of glutamine is accompanied by the hydrolysis of
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase catalyzes: glutamate + NH3 + ATP -> glutamine + ADP + Pi. This reaction consumes one ATP and fixes ammonia in a non-toxic form for transport to the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase consumes ATP to fix ammonia into glutamine amide group

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Glutamine is important.
options: For safe transport of ammonia as the amide nitrogen.
As the major source of ammonia for urinary excretion.
For synthesis of asparagine, purines, and pyrimidines.
questions.explanation: Glutamine serves multiple critical functions: safe ammonia transport (amide nitrogen), ammonia detoxification (brain and muscle), and as nitrogen donor for asparagine, purine, and pyrimidine synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine as safe ammonia carrier and nitrogen donor for nucleotides

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: A genetic defect of an enzyme of urea cycle leads to
questions.explanation: Urea cycle enzyme defects cause hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine (as the body compensatorily shunts ammonia to glutamine synthesis). Blood urea is typically low; ammonia is high.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle defect: high blood glutamine, high ammonia, low urea

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Why may glutamate dehydrogenase be considered a catabolic and not anabolic enzyme?
options: Its Km for ammonia is about ten times the physiological concentration of ammonia.
It is inactivated with high protein intake.
The product of the anabolic direction is not important.
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase has a high Km for ammonia (~10mM, far above physiological levels), meaning it operates primarily in the catabolic direction (deaminating glutamate to release ammonia) under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: High Km of GDH for ammonia makes it primarily catabolic (ammonia-releasing)

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of
questions.explanation: Ammonia is normally used for glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase (the primary ammonia detoxification pathway). The glutamine amide nitrogen is then transported to the liver for urea synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia is normally fixed into glutamine for safe transport and excretion

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Glutaminase reaction is important for which of the following?
options: Releasing ammonia to form urea by liver cells.
Liberation of ammonia in the brain tissue.
Acidification of urine by renal tubular cells.
Detoxification of ammonia in the muscle and nervous tissue.
questions.explanation: Glutaminase in brain tissue liberates ammonia from glutamine, producing glutamate. This is important for brain ammonia metabolism and for providing glutamate for neurotransmitter synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glutaminase releases ammonia in brain tissue from glutamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Glutamic acid is most probably produced by which of the following?
options: Glutamate dehydrogenase at low ammonia concentration.
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate when ammonia concentration is low. At high ammonia, it operates in reverse (catabolic direction).
questions.keyConcept: GDH produces glutamate via amination of alpha-ketoglutarate at low ammonia

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following is a normal flow of nitrogen in human metabolism?
questions.explanation: Valine (amino acid) transaminated to alanine, alanine transaminated to glutamate, glutamate deaminated to release ammonia, and ammonia enters the urea cycle. This describes normal nitrogen flow from amino acid catabolism to urea excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Valine to alanine to glutamate to urea represents normal nitrogen flow

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following passes in the urine of a patient with phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, so phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvic acid, phenyllactic acid, phenylacetylglutamine) accumulate and appear in urine.
questions.keyConcept: PKU causes urinary excretion of phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, and phenylacetylglutamine

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is a mono-oxygenase (mixed function oxygenase) that,
options: Incorporates the two atoms of the oxygen molecule in one substrate molecule.
Necessitates the presence of NADPH-dependent reductase to restore the active cofactor.
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, which gets oxidized to dihydrobiopterin (BH2) during the reaction. NADPH-dependent dihydropteridine reductase must regenerate BH4 for the enzyme to function.
questions.keyConcept: PAH requires BH4 and NADPH-dependent reductase to restore active cofactor

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which enzymatic change explains the slow rate of glycolysis in neurons?
options: High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which inhibits formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
Reduced activity of hexokinase with decreased intracellular glucose
Reduced activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase with decreased fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate (variant)
High activity of 6‑phosphofructo‑2‑kinase which stimulates formation of fructose‑2,6‑bisphosphate
questions.explanation: Neurons have reduced PFK-2/FBPase3 activity, resulting in low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, which inhibits glycolysis and makes neurons dependent on oxidative metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Neuronal glycolytic regulation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: During excessive exercise, which substance serves as an energy source for neurons?
questions.explanation: During excessive exercise, lactate produced by astrocytes serves as an energy source for neurons through the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which statement about ketone bodies is correct?
options: Main energy source for the brain
Main energy source for the liver during starvation
Not a major source of energy in well‑fed state
questions.explanation: Ketone bodies are not a major energy source in the well-fed state; the brain preferentially uses glucose. They become important during starvation when glucose is scarce.
questions.keyConcept: Ketone body utilization states

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: During starvation, which of the following occurs?
options: Ketone bodies are utilized in liver
Ketone bodies are utilized in brain
Fatty acids are utilized in brain
Amino acids are utilized in brain
questions.explanation: During starvation, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) as an alternative fuel when glucose availability decreases.
questions.keyConcept: Starvation brain metabolism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which enzyme is absent in neurons?
questions.explanation: Neurons lack PFK2/FBPase3 (the bifunctional enzyme that produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate), resulting in low glycolytic rate and dependence on oxidative metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Neuronal metabolic enzymes

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which laboratory finding is used as a marker for carcinoid tumor?
questions.explanation: 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main metabolite of serotonin, is elevated in urine and used as a marker for carcinoid tumors that secrete serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid tumor markers

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors.
questions.keyConcept: CNS excitatory neurotransmission

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In pheochromocytoma, which metabolite is typically increased in urine?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumor) causes elevated urinary VMA (vanillylmandelic acid), the main metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: Pheochromocytoma diagnosis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which amino acid is the precursor of serotonin?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan is the precursor amino acid for serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) synthesis via the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin biosynthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which is the rate‑limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase (converting tyrosine to L-DOPA) is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis and requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine synthesis pathway

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: What is the final disposal form of the amino group in the human body?
questions.explanation: Urea is the final disposal form of amino groups in humans, produced in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted in urine.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid nitrogen disposal

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which amino acid becomes essential?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency prevents citrulline formation from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate; arginine becomes essential since the urea cycle cannot complete without it.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle disorders

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The nitrogen atoms of urea are derived from which sources?
questions.explanation: Urea contains two nitrogen atoms: one from ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase reaction).
questions.keyConcept: Urea nitrogen sources

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: A month‑old baby’s urine has a sweet, burnt sugar smell. Elevated leucine, isoleucine, valine. Which enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
questions.keyConcept: Branched-chain amino acid metabolism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which reaction is impaired in thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; its deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine-dependent reactions

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In phenylketonuria, which substance accumulates in the blood?
questions.explanation: PKU results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing accumulation of phenylalanine which is neurotoxic and leads to intellectual disability if untreated.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylketonuria pathophysiology

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which disease and metabolite pair is correctly matched?
options: Maple syrup urine disease and isolysine
Maple syrup urine disease and lysine
Maple syrup urine disease and glycine
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is correctly matched with phenylpyruvate; the disease causes phenylalanine accumulation and its transamination products (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate) are excreted.
questions.keyConcept: PKU metabolite

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: In phenylketonuria, deficiency of which substance occurs?
questions.explanation: In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency leads to inability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, resulting in tyrosine deficiency and catecholamine synthesis impairment.
questions.keyConcept: PKU biochemical defect

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which vitamin is required for one‑carbon transfer reactions involved in nucleotide synthesis?
questions.explanation: Folic acid (as N5, N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate) provides one-carbon units for thymidylate synthase and purine synthesis reactions in nucleotide biosynthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Folate in nucleotide synthesis

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Impairment of oxidative decarboxylation leads to inability to utilize glucose due to deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for oxidative decarboxylation reactions catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine and glucose utilization

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: A patient with chronic diarrhea, cognitive decline, and photosensitive skin rash. Which supplement?
questions.explanation: The triad of diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis (photosensitive rash) is classic for pellagra caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra presentation

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which vitamin deficiency is neurologically affected by folic acid status – folic acid can mask hematological signs but not prevent neurological damage?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord; folic acid can mask the anemia but does not prevent neurological progression.
questions.keyConcept: B12 neurological damage

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which biochemical process is inhibited by sulfonamides?
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis in bacteria (humans obtain folate from diet, not synthesis).
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamide mechanism

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which reaction uses methyltetrahydrofolate as a cofactor?
questions.explanation: Methyltetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
questions.keyConcept: Methyltetrahydrofolate function

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which acts as a coenzyme for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases?
questions.explanation: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the essential cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases including phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases.
questions.keyConcept: Aromatic hydroxylase cofactors

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: The conversion of which requires vitamin B12 and folic acid?
questions.explanation: Homocysteine to methionine conversion requires both vitamin B12 (as methylcobalamin) and folic acid (as methyltetrahydrofolate) for the methionine synthase reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Homocysteine metabolism vitamins

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Management of phenylketonuria necessitates.
options: Early detection by routine neonatal screening.
Starting treatment before the age of 1 month.
questions.explanation: PKU management requires neonatal screening for early detection, low phenylalanine diet (milk substitutes containing tyrosine), and treatment initiation before one month of age to prevent irreversible brain damage.
questions.keyConcept: PKU management: neonatal screening, low Phe diet, early treatment before 1 month

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Why is lactulose given to liver cell failure patients?
options: It is not digested or absorbed, thus has an osmotic laxative effect.
By bacterial action, it produces lactic acid, thus acidifying the intestine.
questions.explanation: Lactulose is not digested or absorbed (osmotic laxative effect) and is metabolized by colonic bacteria to lactic acid and acetic acid, acidifying the colon. This converts NH3 to NH4+ which cannot be absorbed, reducing blood ammonia.
questions.keyConcept: Lactulose acidifies colon to trap NH4+ and reduce ammonia absorption in liver failure

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which of the following would you give to patients with deficient tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism?
questions.explanation: In tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency, phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot function, causing phenylalanine accumulation. Treatment involves supplementing L-dopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan (precursors to dopamine and serotonin) since these pathways also require BH4.
questions.keyConcept: BH4 deficiency treated with L-dopa and 5-HTP precursors bypassing the block

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Which drug prevents the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, preventing conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS, allowing more levodopa to reach the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Levodopa pharmacology

questions.subject: biochem
questions.question: Ethosuximide useful in:
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for absence seizures (petit mal epilepsy). It works by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. Options A and C are incorrect - ethosuximide does NOT work for partial epilepsy or tonic-clonic seizures. Option D is wrong - ethosuximide is not useful for combined absence and tonic-clonic (valproate is preferred for mixed seizures). For absence seizures only: ethosuximide or valproate; for absence plus tonic-clonic: valproate is preferred. Answer is B - ethosuximide is specifically useful in absence seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment for absence seizures, acting via T-type calcium channel blockade.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which substance acts as an antioxidant in astrocytes by forming reduced glutathione?
questions.explanation: NADPH in astrocytes provides reducing equivalents for the glutathione reductase system, converting GSSG to reduced glutathione (GSH) to combat oxidative stress.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte antioxidant systems

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: What are the microscopic features of Ependymomas?
options: Uniform small cells, round to oval nuclei with granular chromatin
Highly cellular with marked nuclear atypia
questions.explanation: Ependymoma microscopic features include: perivascular pseudorosettes (tumor cells arranged around blood vessels with fibrillary processes) and true ependymal rosettes (tumor cells arranged around central lumen). The cells have uniform, round to oval nuclei. The answer is A. Perivascular pseudorosettes are the most distinctive feature. GFAP is positive.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymomas show perivascular pseudorosettes and true rosettes - diagnostic histological features.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: What are the three most common neuroepithelial brain tumors in children?
questions.explanation: The three most common neuroepithelial brain tumors in children are: pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I, cerebellar, good prognosis), medulloblastoma (WHO grade IV, cerebellar, highly malignant), and ependymoma (WHO grade II-III, from ependymal cells). Option A is CORRECT. Glioblastoma and anaplastic astrocytoma (B) are adult tumors. Oligodendroglioma (C) is also more common in adults. Meningioma and schwannoma (D) are adult tumors. The answer is A.
questions.keyConcept: Children's most common brain tumors are pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, and ependymoma - all in the posterior fossa.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The following tumor arises from the lining of the ventricular system:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells that line the ventricular system and central canal of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma arises from ependymal lining of ventricular system

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Astrocytoma is a:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are glial tumors derived from astrocytes, the most common primary brain tumors. They range from grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, highly malignant).
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma is a glial tumor (from astrocytes)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Oligodendrogliomas are not characterized by:
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK).
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas do NOT typically show activation of the MAPK pathway. They characteristically have IDH1/IDH2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion. MAPK activation is seen in pilocytic astrocytomas (BRAF fusion).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion (NOT MAPK activation) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following factors depress synaptic transmission?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia depresses synaptic transmission by impairing the energy-dependent processes required for neurotransmitter synthesis and the Na+/K+ ATPase maintaining membrane potential.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia depresses synaptic transmission by impairing energy-dependent processes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: As regards pons, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: Cerebello-pontine angle gives attachment to VI & VII cranial nerves.
Nervus intermedius is the medial root of the facial nerve.
VIII cranial nerve lies medial to VII cranial nerve.
Its ventral surface shows a sulcus for vertebral artery.
questions.explanation: Cerebellopontine angle tumors typically arise from the vestibulocochlear nerve (acoustic neuroma/schwannoma) and cause hearing loss, vertigo, and later facial nerve involvement. Pontine gliomas would cause different symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: CPA tumors cause deafness and vertigo

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Gliosis means:
questions.explanation: Gliosis is the proliferation of glial cells (particularly astrocytes) in response to CNS injury. It represents a protective/scarring response rather than true regeneration. Brain tissue cannot regenerate neurons, so gliosis forms a glial scar. Option A (regeneration) is wrong because neurons don't regenerate in CNS. Option B (necrosis) is the cause of gliosis, not gliosis itself. Option C (fibrosis) occurs in other tissues but not brain - brain forms glial (astrocytic) scars, not fibrous scars. The correct answer is D (None of the above) because gliosis specifically means proliferation of neuroglial cells as a response to CNS injury, which is neither regeneration nor fibrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Gliosis is astrocyte proliferation forming a glial scar in response to CNS injury, not true regeneration or fibrosis.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Contralateral representation of face and body is found in:
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory and motor cortices have contralateral representation (homunculus). The face representation is in the lateral hemisphere near the Sylvian fissure, while body representation is medial near the longitudinal fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Cortical representation is somatotopically organized with contralateral control for both motor and sensory functions.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: What is responsible for the conscious discrimination of odors?
options: Lateral & VM hypothalamus, septum, Amygdala, thalamus & basal ganglia
questions.explanation: Conscious odor discrimination is mediated by the orbitofrontal and frontal neocortex, which receives processed olfactory information via thalamic relays, allowing identification and naming of odors.
questions.keyConcept: Neocortical olfactory discrimination

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system due to its connections with:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system, and the reticular formation modulates hypothalamic function.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation → hypothalamus → pituitary → endocrine control. RF also influences autonomic functions via hypothalamus.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The apical surface of ependymal Cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Purkinje layer is a layer of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex layers are: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), multiform (VI).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex 6 layers: I molecular, II external granular, III external pyramidal, IV internal granular, V internal pyramidal, VI multiform. Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All of the following are cells of the cerebral cortex except:
questions.explanation: All of these - pyramidal cells, granular cells, fusiform cells, and Martinotti cells - ARE cells of the cerebral cortex. Pyramidal cells are the most common excitatory neurons. Granular cells are small interneurons. Fusiform cells are in the deep layer. Martinotti cells have ascending axons.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex neurons: pyramidal (main), granular, fusiform, Martinotti, basket, Chandelier cells.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Martinotti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells are characterized by being inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of the cerebral cortex. They have axons that ascend to the molecular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells are inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of cerebral cortex

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Dura matter characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Dura mater is a fibrous, avascular layer (contains few blood vessels). It forms the outermost meninx. Arachnoid has trabeculae; pia is vascular; arachnoid barrier layer is cellular. Dura's toughness comes from collagen fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: tough outer meninx, fibrous, relatively avascular; attached to periosteum of skull/vertebrae.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Concerning the pia matter, which of the following statements is true:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is highly vascular (contains blood vessels that penetrate to supply superficial brain tissue). It is the innermost meninx, in direct contact with brain. Arachnoid contains spaces (subarachnoid) for CSF, not pia. Dura contains venous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater: highly vascular, innermost meninx, follows brain contours closely.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the brain-CSF barrier, limiting passage between ventricles and brain parenchyma. The blood-brain barrier involves astrocyte foot processes and tight junction endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal tight junctions = brain-CSF barrier. Astrocyte foot processes + endothelial tight junctions = blood-brain barrier.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Endothelial cells of blood capillaries in brain characterized by having:
questions.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles (not more), abundant mitochondria (for transport functions), tight junctions (not few), and few desmosomes. Tight junctions are essential for the blood-brain barrier function.
questions.keyConcept: Brain endothelium: tight junctions, few pinocytic vesicles (blood-brain barrier)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which statement is true regarding neuroglia?
options: Schwann cells are found in the CNS
Ependymal cells form nodes of Ranvier
questions.explanation: Astrocytes perform gliosis (reactive astrogliosis) in response to CNS injury, forming glial scars; they also maintain the blood-brain barrier and ion balance.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte functions

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is involved in the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are involved in the blood-brain barrier, through their end-feet which induce and maintain tight junctions between endothelial cells. Ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, not the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following is a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by the choroid plexus epithelium (border cells of arachnoid matter - actually choroid plexus cells), not ependymal cells. Ependymal cells line ventricles. The barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries + choroid plexus epithelium with tight junctions.
questions.keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: choroid plexus epithelium + fenestrated capillaries + tight junctions.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by.
questions.explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (which faces the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is attached to periosteum. This creates the dural sinus spaces between the two layers.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: outer surface = periosteum; inner surface = simple squamous mesothelium facing arachnoid.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The brain CSF barrier is not formed of:
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.
questions.explanation: The brain-CSF barrier is formed by ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes. Fenestrated endothelial cells are NOT part of this barrier - the brain capillary endothelium has tight junctions forming the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Brain-CSF barrier: ependymal tight junctions + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The blood CSF barrier is not formed of:
options: Endothelial cells of fenestrated blood capillaries
Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.
questions.explanation: Foot processes of astrocytes are part of the BLOOD-BRAIN barrier, not the blood-CSF barrier. The blood-CSF barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries, basement membrane, and choroid plexus epithelium (connected by tight junctions).
questions.keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: fenestrated capillaries + choroid epithelium with tight junctions. Blood-brain barrier: tight junction endothelium + astrocyte foot processes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by:
questions.explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (the epidural boundary facing the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is also lined by mesothelium.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater inner surface lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A 9-year-old child has enlargement of the lateral ventricles with a 4 cm homogenous well-circumscribed mass within the 4th ventricle. Microscopically, it shows rosettes & pseudo-rosettes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system, especially common in children in the 4th ventricle. They show both rosettes (true ependymal rosettes) and pseudorosettes (perivascular).
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma: rosettes and pseudorosettes, 4th ventricle in children

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is involved in the blood brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes form the blood-brain barrier through their foot processes surrounding CNS capillaries, regulating molecular passage into the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes in BBB

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesothelial cells), a single layer that closely invests the brain and spinal cord surface.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater composition

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Six hours after a meal, which of the following is (are) MOST important as a source of fuel for the brain?
options: Fatty acids from the adipose tissue.
questions.explanation: After 6 hours post-meal (fasting state), the brain relies primarily on ketone bodies (from hepatic fatty acid oxidation) as its main fuel. Glycogen stores are depleted. Fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently. Protein is not a primary brain fuel.
questions.keyConcept: Brain fuel: glucose (fed) → ketone bodies (fasting). Ketone bodies cross BBB and replace glucose after prolonged fasting.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Brain cells uptake glucose by
questions.explanation: Brain cells uptake glucose via GLUT1 (blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (neurons); GLUT2 is in liver/pancreas, GLUT4 is insulin-dependent in muscle/adipose.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glucose transporters

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Glucose uptake by the brain is
questions.explanation: Brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent; GLUT1 and GLUT3 are constitutively active at the blood-brain barrier and neuronal membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Insulin-independent brain glucose uptake

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Brain cells uptake glucose by:
questions.explanation: Brain cells take up glucose via GLUT1 (on the blood-brain barrier, constitutive) and GLUT3 (on neurons, high affinity). GLUT2 is in liver and pancreas; GLUT4 is insulin-dependent (muscle/fat); GLUT5 is a fructose transporter; SGLT2 is in kidney.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glucose uptake by GLUT1 (BBB) and GLUT3 (neurons)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given:
questions.explanation: L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase, increasing catecholamine levels in Parkinson's patients with dopaminergic neuron loss. Alpha-methyldopa is an antihypertensive.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa administered to increase brain catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the arachnoid granulations?
options: They absorb cerebrospinal fluid into the venous system.
questions.explanation: Arachnoid granulations (Pacchionian bodies) are herniations of arachnoid mater into dural venous sinuses that absorb cerebrospinal fluid into the venous system.
questions.keyConcept: Arachnoid granulations absorb CSF into venous sinuses.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which glucose transporter is present on astrocytes?
questions.explanation: GLUT1 is the glucose transporter predominantly expressed on astrocytes and the blood-brain barrier, facilitating glucose entry into the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte glucose transport

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A 5-year-old girl diagnosed with meningitis. The doctor prescribes her antibiotics. Which of the following statements should be considered true?
options: The blood brain barrier normally allows the passage of all antibiotics.
The blood brain barrier does not allow the passage of antibiotics due to their big molecular size.
The systemic administration of penicillin normally results in large amount entering CNS.
The meninges become more permeable to penicillin at the site of inflammation and its concentration rises in cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.explanation: In meningitis, inflamed meninges become more permeable allowing increased penicillin entry; normal BBB restricts many antibiotics from CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Meningitis and antibiotic penetration

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Sensations received by the thalamus include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus acts as a relay station for almost all sensory modalities (except olfaction) on their way to the cerebral cortex. It receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations. Olfaction (smell) is the only sensory modality that does not relay through the thalamus—olfactory signals go directly to the olfactory bulb and limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: All major sensations relay through thalamus EXCEPT smell; olfactory pathway bypasses thalamus to limbic system.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A 28‑year‑old woman has unilateral tinnitus, vertigo, and progressive hearing loss. MRI reveals a 3 cm mass at the cerebellopontine angle. Which microscopic finding is most characteristic?
options: Whorled spindle cells with psammoma bodies
Hypo‑ and hypercellular areas (Antoni A and B)
questions.explanation: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at cerebellopontine angle shows Antoni A (cellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular) areas with verocay bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular schwannoma

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The medial surface of thalamus:
options: Is limited inferiorly by hypothalamic sulcus.
Is connected to the opposite surface by interthalamic adhesions.
questions.explanation: The medial surface of the thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle, is limited inferiorly by the hypothalamic sulcus, and the two thalami are connected in about 80% of individuals by an interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia). All the listed statements about the medial surface are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Medial surface of thalamus: forms lateral wall of 3rd ventricle, bounded below by hypothalamic sulcus, connected to opposite thalamus by interthalamic adhesion.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Martinoti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells have axons directed UPWARDS (toward the cortical surface). Their dendrites extend laterally, cell bodies are multipolar (not rounded), and they use various neurotransmitters. They are inhibitory interneurons in the cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells: cortical interneurons with ascending axons; deliver inhibitory signals to superficial layers.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Extracranial headache is an example of:
questions.explanation: Extracranial headache originates from structures outside the cranium such as muscles, vessels, or nerves in the scalp and face (e.g., tension headache, cluster headache).
questions.keyConcept: Extracranial headaches arise from pericranial structures; intracranial headaches involve meninges or blood vessels.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: About spinal nerve all true except:
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion:
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.
questions.explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.
Have shwann cells around its cell bodies.
questions.explanation: DRG cells are pseudounipolar with multiple processes (one peripheral, one central). They have eccentric nuclei, are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers, and are surrounded by satellite glial cells (not Schwann cells around the cell body itself).
questions.keyConcept: DRG cells: pseudounipolar, multiple processes, eccentric nucleus, satellite cells, myelinated + unmyelinated fibers.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following cells Produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons). Schwann cells do this in the PNS. Astrocytes provide support; satellite cells support neurons in ganglia; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (multiple axons). Schwann cells: PNS myelin (one axon each).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in injury and disease to phagocytose debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages (phagocytic), mesodermal origin, activated in injury/disease.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein specific to astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in histology and neuropathology. Oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells do not contain GFAP.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP: astrocyte marker (intermediate filament). Used to identify astrocytes in CNS.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The outer band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL GRANULAR layer (layer IV). This band represents dense termination of thalamocortical fibers. The inner band of Baillarger is in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V).
questions.keyConcept: Outer Baillarger: layer IV (internal granular) - thalamocortical input. Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The cytoplasm of astrocytes contains
questions.explanation: Astrocytes contain microtubules (for transport), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein - their intermediate filament marker), and thread-like mitochondria. These contents help identify astrocytes histologically. GFAP is the most specific marker.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte cytoplasm: GFAP (marker), microtubules, mitochondria. GFAP used for astrocyte identification.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion?
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following nuclei is not present in all segments of the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning the lateral horn of the spinal cord is TRUE?
options: Gives origin to pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers.
It is most prominent at sacral levels.
It is present in all spinal cord levels.
questions.explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Anterior horn of spinal cord contains the following nuclei EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei. There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei: anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral (no 'middle' nucleus) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The second order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.
