questions.explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillar acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein found specifically in astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in tissue and in astrocytoma diagnostics.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP is the specific marker for astrocytes (intermediate filament protein)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The following tumor shows a whorly pattern of growth:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas characteristically show a whorled pattern of growth with spindle cells and psammoma bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma shows whorled pattern of growth

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Glioblastoma multiforme shows:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows vascular proliferation (neovascularization with abnormal vessels), necrosis with pseudopalisading, and highly anaplastic cells. Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; rosette formation in medulloblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: vascular proliferation (not Rosenthal fibers or rosettes)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei has motor function?
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nucleus (in the anterior horn) has motor function, containing motor neuron pools for axial and proximal limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: An 18-year-old male presents with a well-circumscribed mass involving the 4th ventricle. Diagnostic microscopical findings in this condition include:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas show both rosettes (true ependymal) and pseudorosettes (perivascular). Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; Verocay bodies in schwannomas; chicken wire calcification in oligodendrogliomas.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma: rosettes and pseudorosettes (not Rosenthal fibers or Verocay bodies)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Astrocytoma is:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are tumors derived from astrocytes, classified as grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, malignant). They are the most common primary brain tumors, typically in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma: glial tumor from astrocytes, grades I-IV

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Meningioma shows:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are characterized by psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions), whorled patterns of spindle cells, and meningothelial cells. Rosenthal fibers are seen in pilocytic astrocytomas; vascular proliferation in glioblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma characteristic: psammoma bodies, whorled pattern

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are present in lamina «.. of spinal cord gray matter:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, corresponding to lamina VII of Rexed. Parasympathetic neurons are in sacral segments (S2-S4), not thoracic lamina II.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in lateral horn (lamina VII, T1-L2/3)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which structure is found in lamina I of the spinal cord gray matter?
questions.explanation: The posteromarginal nucleus is located in lamina I of the spinal cord and receives pain and temperature afferents from the periphery.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord lamina I

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All the following characters of Golgi Cell except:
options: dendrite extend in all cortex layer
its axon in granular layers that synapse with granular cell
its dendrite in golgi layer only
questions.explanation: Golgi cells have large cell bodies with many long dendrites that extend into all cortical layers (not just the Golgi layer), and their axons synapse with granular cells in the granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi cell characteristics

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Border cell attached by:
questions.explanation: Border cells (meningothelial cells) between arachnoid and dura are attached by both tight junctions and desmosomes for structural integrity.
questions.keyConcept: Border cell junctions

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Type of junction between endothelium or ependymal:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between endothelial cells and ependymal cells create the selective permeability barrier in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junction function

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells) that is partially ciliated, similar to the ventricular lining.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal epithelium

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Myelination inside the CNS depends on:
questions.explanation: Myelination in the CNS is performed by oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelination: oligodendrocytes (PNS: Schwann cells).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of thoracic level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Thoracic spinal cord has lateral horns (intermediolateral cell columns) containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons, giving it 4 horns.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic spinal cord

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in proprioception from the lower body have cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia) at corresponding levels.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first neuron lower body

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The second order neuron in proprioception from lower half of the body is in:
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for lower body proprioception are in the gracile nucleus on the same side, which then decussates as internal arcuate fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception second neuron lower

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following is true about cuneate tract:
options: It arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on same side.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on opposite side.
It is present in lateral column of white matter in spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia in the upper half of the body (cervical and upper thoracic) and carries upper limb proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract origin

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Tic douloureux:
options: Is due to convergence facilitation theory.
Is due to sensitization of pain receptors by chemicals.
Sharp lancinating pain in the distribution of the facial nerve.
Is an example of secondary hyperalgesia.
questions.explanation: Tic douloureux (trigeminal neuralgia) causes sharp, lancinating facial pain due to trigeminal nerve dysfunction, often triggered by innocuous stimuli like touching the face.
questions.keyConcept: Tic douloureux: sharp lancinating pain in trigeminal distribution.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Athetosis is associated with movement which is NOT:
questions.explanation: Athetosis movements are NOT decreased by emotions - they increase with emotional states. Option E is correct. Athetosis consists of slow, twisting, spontaneous movements that intensify with emotional stress, fatigue, and attempts at voluntary movement. Option A, B, C, D all correctly describe athetoid movements.
questions.keyConcept: Athetoid movements intensify with emotional states and voluntary attempts, distinguishing them from other movement disorders.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Spinal shock produces:-
questions.explanation: Spinal shock produces hypotension. Option B is correct. Loss of sympathetic outflow after spinal cord transection causes vasodilation and hypotension. Options A, C, D describe later effects (automatic micturition after shock, positive Babinski develops later, spasticity develops weeks later). During spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, loss of bowel/bladder, hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Acute spinal shock causes flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and hypotension due to loss of sympathetic tone.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Long-term effects of cord trans-section at T12 include:
options: Loss of tendon jerks in lower limbs.
Hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs.
questions.explanation: Long-term cord transection at T12: hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs. Option D is correct. After spinal shock resolves, UMN signs develop below the lesion (weeks to months). Options A, B, C are incorrect: bladder paralysis is not typical (autonomic dysreflexia occurs), tendon jerks are exaggerated (not lost), hyperalgesia is not typical.
questions.keyConcept: After spinal shock resolves, transection above T12 causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia in lower limbs.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
options: They are larger and more numerous than gamma neurons.
They supply extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.
Alpha in the lateral part of anterior horn are concerned with fine movements
Alpha of flexors are dorsally present to alpha of extensors
All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit.
questions.explanation: All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit - this is NOT true. Option E is INCORRECT. Multiple alpha motor neurons innervate a single muscle; each alpha neuron with its fibers constitutes ONE motor unit, not all alpha cells. Option A is wrong (alpha are larger, not more numerous). Option B is true (supply extrafusal). Option C is true (lateral horn for fine movements). Option D is wrong (flexor alphas are rostral to extensor).
questions.keyConcept: Motor units are individual alpha motor neurons plus all muscle fibers they innervate; many motor units compose a single muscle.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Regarding the stretch reflex, which sentence is NOT true:
options: Can be elicited by passive stretch.
Depends on the muscle spindle which is a mechanoreceptor present parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Stretch of a muscle is followed by its contraction.
Is associated with simultaneous inhibition of the antagonist muscle.
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is a polysynaptic reflex - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Stretch reflex is MONOsynaptic (one synapse between Ia afferent and alpha motor neuron). Options A, B, D, E are correct: elicited by passive stretch, depends on spindle parallel to extrafusal, causes muscle contraction, inhibits antagonists.
questions.keyConcept: The stretch reflex is the prototypical monosynaptic reflex with a single excitatory synapse.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (approximately -70 mV in neurons) closely matches the equilibrium potential of K+ (approximately -90 mV) because the membrane at rest is most permeable to potassium.
questions.keyConcept: The resting membrane potential approximates the K+ equilibrium potential due to high resting K+ permeability.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Concerning synapses:
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs & chemicals
In chemical synapses, gap junction conduct impulses between presynaptic & postsynaptic structure
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are widely distributed in the CNS, not rare. Electric synapses are characterized by rapid transmission without delay, are bidirectional (not unidirectional), and do not use gap junctions in the typical chemical synaptic cleft.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses: neurotransmitter-based, drug-sensitive, unidirectional, wide distribution in CNS.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The mechanism of synaptic transmission includes:
options: Ca++ ions are released from the presynaptic knob
Presynaptic knobs release only an excitatory transmitter
Chemical transmission causes development of only excitatory postsynaptic state
Excitatory transmitters hyperpolarize the postsynaptic membrane
The released transmitter combines with specific receptors on postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation: Ca++ ions enter the presynaptic terminal (not released from it) to trigger vesicle fusion. Presynaptic knobs release both excitatory and inhibitory transmitters. Transmitters cause either EPSPs or IPSPs. Excitatory transmitters cause depolarization (not hyperpolarization).
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic transmission: Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis; transmitter binds specific receptors causing EPSP or IPSP.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:
questions.explanation: Kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) are released during tissue damage and are potent pain-producing substances. They sensitize nociceptors. ATP also contributes but kinins are the primary algogenic substance among these options.
questions.keyConcept: Pain mediators: bradykinin, histamine, serotonin, ATP, prostaglandins - released from damaged tissue.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons that supply a specific muscle do NOT represent one motor unit; a motor unit is one alpha motor neuron plus ALL the muscle fibers it innervates. Multiple alpha neurons contribute to each muscle. The statement is false because it contradicts the definition of motor unit.
questions.keyConcept: Motor unit = 1 α-motor neuron + all muscle fibers it innervates; one muscle has many motor units.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Physiologically, an intact innervated muscle can normally be made to contract by stimulation of which of the following neurons innervating that muscle?
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers and are the final common pathway for muscle contraction. Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers and adjust spindle sensitivity but cannot directly cause visible muscle contraction.
questions.keyConcept: α-motor neurons: final pathway for skeletal muscle contraction; γ-motor neurons: adjust spindle sensitivity.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which sentence is NOT true regarding consolidation of memory:
options: It is the conversion of short-term memory to a long-term one.
Represents the time needed for the structural and functional synaptic changes to take place.
Increases and fastens by focusing and rehearsal.
questions.explanation: Consolidation takes much longer than 5 minutes - it can take hours to days. Consolidation is the conversion of STM to LTM through synaptic changes and takes time for structural modifications. Completed in 5 minutes is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Memory consolidation: conversion of STM to LTM; takes hours-days; requires protein synthesis.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Concerning synapses, which of the following is true?
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS.
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission.
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse.
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs and chemicals.
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are the most common type in the CNS and are susceptible to modulation by neurotransmitters, drugs, and toxins. Electrical synapses allow direct ionic coupling and are bidirectional.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are the predominant CNS synapse type and are targetable by drugs unlike electrical synapses.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Postsynaptic inhibition in the CNS is primarily mediated by which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A receptors to cause chloride influx and hyperpolarization.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, mediating most fast synaptic inhibition.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which explains areas with low two-point discrimination threshold?
options: Less convergence of afferent nerve fibers
More convergence of afferent nerve fibers
questions.explanation: Areas with low two-point discrimination threshold (high resolution) like fingertips have higher cortical representation in the sensory homunculus. Smaller receptive fields and greater receptor density enable finer discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Two-point discrimination inversely correlates with receptive field size and cortical magnification factor.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which statement regarding sensory fiber conduction is correct?
options: Crude touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Fine touch is carried on C fibers
Fine touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Vibration sense is carried on Aδ fibers
Nociceptive stimuli are carried on Aβ fibers
questions.explanation: Sensory fiber conduction velocity correlates with fiber diameter: A-delta fibers (5-15 m/s) transmit fast pain; C fibers (0.5-2 m/s) transmit slow pain. Myelination increases conduction velocity.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction velocity in sensory fibers depends on diameter and myelination: A-delta > C fibers.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Sudden increase in skin temperature above 50 °C leads to:
options: Transient impulses due to damage of cold receptors above 40 °C
questions.explanation: Heat above 50C stimulates thermal nociceptors (via TRPV1 channels) causing burning pain. Temperatures above 45C begin to activate pain receptors, with noxious heat stimulating C and A-delta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: TRPV1 receptors on nociceptors respond to temperatures above 43-45C, triggering burning pain sensation.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which substance stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Bradykinin, substance P, histamine, prostaglandins, and serotonin are all algogenic substances that stimulate nociceptors and cause pain when released during tissue injury or inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Algogenic substances (bradykinin, prostaglandins, substance P) sensitize and activate nociceptors.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which clinical sign is seen in chronic gastritis due to inflammation of the stomach wall?
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis causing inflammation of the stomach body (where parietal cells are located) leads to loss of intrinsic factor and reduced acid production, resulting in pernicious anemia with neurological manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal cell destruction in body gastritis causes intrinsic factor deficiency and pernicious anemia.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Acupuncture relieves pain mainly by:
options: Gate control theory and psychogenic excitation
Blockade of sodium channels in sensory nerves
questions.explanation: Acupuncture relieves pain primarily by stimulating A-beta fibers that activate descending inhibitory pathways from PAG to nucleus raphe magnus, releasing endogenous opioids.
questions.keyConcept: Acupuncture activates descending inhibitory pathways via A-beta fiber stimulation and endogenous opioid release.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The initial phase of a migraine attack is associated with which vascular event?
questions.explanation: The initial phase of migraine involves cortical spreading depression followed by vasoconstriction causing the aura. Later phases involve vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Migraine starts with cortical spreading depression and vasoconstriction (aura), followed by vasodilation causing headache.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which pattern of sensory loss is characteristic of peripheral neuritis?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuritis causes stocking-glove sensory loss (distal symmetric loss) affecting all sensory modalities due to length-dependent axonal degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Peripheral neuritis produces symmetric distal sensory loss in stocking-glove distribution from length-dependent neuropathy.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The memory of a sequence of events in which a person participated is called:
questions.explanation: Episodic memory records personal experiences organized in time sequence (autobiographical memory), allowing recall of events in which one actively participated.
questions.keyConcept: Episodic memory: memory of personal events in sequence.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Semantic memory is characterized by which of the following?
options: It is the memory of personal events
It is the memory of facts
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is explicit/declarative memory for facts and knowledge about the world (general facts), distinct from episodic memory (personal events) and procedural memory (skills).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory: memory of facts (general knowledge).

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Semantic memory refers to:
options: Memory of facts and general knowledge
questions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general facts, concepts, and knowledge independent of personal experience (declarative/explicit memory).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that increases the permeability of the postsynaptic membrane to which ion?
questions.explanation: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels; chloride influx hyperpolarizes the neuron, causing inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: GABA mechanism

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Fast pain (first pain) is transmitted to the CNS by which fibres?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers (myelinated, fast-conducting) transmit first/quick pain, while C fibers (unmyelinated) transmit slow, throbbing second pain.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain fibers

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following is purely sensory?
questions.explanation: The dorsal root of the spinal nerve is purely sensory, containing afferent fibers from the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor/efferent. The mixed spinal nerve trunk and its rami contain both sensory and motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root = purely sensory
